THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Oral History
Interview with Jimmy Jones by Patricia Willard
Reel 1
December 21-23, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
rfm
P R O C E E D I N G S
This is December 21st, 1977, and this is the oral history with Jimmy Jones, whose full name is what?
James Henry Jones, Jr.
Oh. And do people call you mostly Jimmy Jones, or there are some people that call you James Jones, aren't there?
My family, they say James. They don't accept the professional name. But everybody else says Jimmy. So consequently, you know, I've gotten adjusted to both.
Uh-huh.
I can always tell who's behind me, saying which name, and I say, "Oh, that's somebody in the family," or, "That's somebody I work with."
(Laughter)
What is your birthdate?
December the 30th -- gee, I've got one coming up this year.
In a couple of weeks. Less than a couple of weeks.
Yes. 1918. You see me hesitate on the 18?
Why?
I don't know. I don't know. It's just
Yeah, they have a way of speeding up.
You know? So my mother gave a 1919 date for an insurance policy, which I don't know whether it's true or not, but I guess the rates were down, so --
Well, you have a birth certificate, don't you?
No.
You don't?
Isn't that amazing? I think I can get one. I know exactly where I was born. I know the house and everything, but it got lost in the shuffle along the way.
Hasn't that ever -- well, you've been overseas, haven't you? Or have you? Haven't you needed one for a passport?
They didn't require it. I have the passport.
As far as you know you were born in 1918.
Yes. Now, if you want to put it up to 1928, I'd appreciate that.
(Laughter)
You were born where?
Memphis, Tennessee. And my family moved

to Chicago. My father was a professor, an English professor, you know, at Le Moine (PHONETIC) College in Memphis. In fact he taught Jimmy Lunceford English, before Lunceford went to Fisk University in Nashville. And then we moved to Chicago when I was, oh, maybe five, four or five, right around the kindergarten stage.
What do you remember from Memphis?

Nothing. Not at that age. But when I went back, and they gave my father kind of a homecoming, and the faculty there, you know. I'll tell you, the most impressed thing that really got to me was the -- it was highly integrated then.
In Memphis?
Yeah.
Tennessee?
Yeah. I was only nine years old then, and my father -- well, the old man was a great student at Fisk, and --
Was that where he graduated from?

Uh-huh. And he went back and they treated him like a king. And that's the only thing I remember, other than the one time I worked with Sarah Vaughan, and of course I have a lot of relatives there. One was a school principal and the other one was a school teacher. You know, that was the thing in those days.
Now are you talking about the time
your father was honored at Fisk or at Le Moine?
No, at Le Moine.
At Le Moine.
Yeah. The faculty there.
And that was when you were nine, so that would be about 1927.
Yeah, just before the Depression hit.
Uh-huh.

And I remember how nice people were. It was a great experience. And the old man was proud to take me around and show me off, you know. And I really didn't know that he was a violin player. I knew he was a choir director. And when he passed all he had mainly was a bunch of big scores. "The Hallelujah Chorus," and those standard things of years ago, you know?
Uh-huh.

But I came home with a violin out of a pawnshop one day, and I saw the name Stradivarius on it. But I didn't see the word imitation. And my father just looked at me and picked it up and started playing it.
How old were you then?

I was going to junior college in Chicago. I guess I must have been about 17, maybe. 17 -- maybe about 17 years old. And I guess it was inevitable that I would probably end up with someone like Stuff Smith, because the
violin always fascinated me.
Uh-huh.
You know?
And that was the first time your father ever played violin in front of you?
Yeah. Yeah.
What did it date back to? Did you ask him, when --

No, he just picked it up and said, "No, James." I had a -- oh, a little discussion with another student. He said, "Man, that's not a Stradivarius. It can't be." You know. So I was in my ego trip, and I said, "Yes, it is. It says so on here." So I took it home and my father told me the same thing. He said, "No, James, this is not a Stradivarius," and picked it up and started playing it. You know.
He didn't tell you whether -- where he had learned or when he had played it before?
No. I didn't know he was the honor student that he was until his service, his funeral, you know? He was just very -- he was a modest man. He just never said anything about it.
Was there music in your home? I mean did anybody play?
Oh, yes, my mother played piano. She
could sight read on piano. And my father, oh, yeah, he did a lot of choir directing around Chicago in those days, you know?
Did he do any choir directing in Memphis, or was it when he got to Chicago?
No, both places, you know. And then --
Where? Do you remember the names of the churches, or was it churches that he directed?
Yeah, church choirs. One was -- oh, it was a Congregational church. We called it Good Shepherd. A beautiful church, you know.
Was that Chicago?

Uh-huh. Now, before then I just didn't -- I knew that he had done this, because my family -- the other part of my family in Memphis had told me all about that. And then I began to do research on my father, because he just never said. You know, just took everything for granted. And of course my mother was a great support to him. We had our ups and downs and whatever, but it all turned out quite well. I really appreciate -- oh, how can I say this -- the things that they told me when I was in my early teens still work today.
What kind of things?
Oh, like you're disciplined with yourself. Your desire to do something worthwhile, no matter what's going on. Just stay on top of your own case, keep
going. And I just wish they could -- they really laid the foundation for me. I wish they could have been around now to see that it has turned out pretty good.
Uh-huh.

That's the only regret I have, now, you know, the ones that laid the foundation are not here. You know? But if I want to fantasize I might say that they saw something that in the future, you know, they saw something. But they were able to guide me right.
Your father was James Henry Jones, Sr.
Senior, yeah.
Your mother's name was what?
Mary -- well, I'll give you her maiden name.
All right.
Mary Genevra Young.
How do you spell Genevra?
Well, let me see. I've got to think about that, do it phonetically. G-e-n-e-v-r-a.
Just the way it sounds.
Yeah. Just phonetically, you know. So --
Had she studied music?
Uh-huh.
Where? Did she have a private teacher?

Yeah. In those days they were private teachers. But you could put a sheet of music in front of her on the piano and she could sight read it. You know? Some music was around the house since I was a tot, you know. I had -- I tried to study something else and I went that way, did a lot of studying in science in high school, and sociology at Kentucky State University, but the music was where it was.
Did she teach you music? Or where did --
No, they sent me to a private teacher, a neighborhood teacher.
At what age?

Oh, I must have been -- now you're -- I have to think back awhile, now. I started up with guitar, a little four stringed guitar, and then I graduated over to the piano. I guess I must have been about eight or nine years old.
When you first started playing the four stringed guitar?
No, when I started playing piano.
Well, how old were you when you started playing the guitar?
Let's see, I was still in grammar school. Oh, maybe about -- well, maybe about six or seven years old.
How did you happen to start playing guitar at that age, and how come it was guitar that you started playing first?

Now, let me -- let me think awhile. Got to get my head together here. Oh, I know. Yeah, I can associate it now. At that time the Mills Brothers, they were very popular, and this is before John Mills died, you know, and all the kids around Chicago, we all had little quartet singing groups, because these guys were great inspirations, a great inspiration to all of us, you know? And everybody -- well, it was really a ukalele. Wait a minute. Now that you asked me. It started out with a ukalele, into four stringed guitar, then to six stringed guitar, into piano.
Uh-huh.
And each thing began to develop until whatever it became, you know? And --
Do you remember how you happened to pick the ukalele first?
Well, it was the cheapest and the most available, if I can put it that way.
Sure.
So, you know, those --
Did you have any help on what to do with the ukalele once you got it?
Now, let me see, who taught me this?
I can't remember. I don't even remember how I learned how to play. But I got some books. They would have diagram books, you know.
Uh-huh.
Where to put your fingers on the strings to get the certain sounds. And --
But your first actual instruction was on the piano, right?
Oh, yes. That was formal.
I see. The reason -- one of the reasons I'm interested in this particularly is that -- you know Brooks Kerr (ABOMINIC), don't you? The young pianist in New York who's the Ellington specialist?
Oh, yes, I know of him.
Yeah. Well, Brooks is 25 years old and Brooks told me that he's always been fascinated by your playing.
Well, that's good to hear.

And he said that he was talking to another pianist -- and I forget whom he said it was -- and they were talking about your particular approach to the piano and how distinctive it is and how you play -- your concepts are different than any other pianist they've ever heard, and they were trying to figure out why and how you approach chords and chord progressions, and so Brooks said,

"The closest we could come was that we had heard that Jimmy Jones used to play guitar, and we were wondering if maybe he approaches the piano as a guitarist." Now, is that possible? Does that make sense to you?
Yeah, I think so.
Because he said --
As I look back on myself, it's just transferring the notes from one instrument to another.
So you thought guitar first and you still -- well, you still approach it somewhat as --
No, not now. See that --
But that had something to do with your original --
Yeah.
-- approach.

And of course the foundation is still there, you know. You never lose that. But as you grow and develop and begin to add things on and widen your scope, I think -- I don't know whether I could do it like I used to do it, now. I couldn't hold still, because I went to school and started learning more, and learning more, and learning more. Things advance, you know? You have to stay on top of it.
When you started playing piano, was it because you found piano more interesting than the guitar or the ukalele?
A bigger challenge.
Uh-huh.

And there's a -- you know, I got a piano bug, just like guys get a golf bug. I've had a golf bug at one time. I would come home with my books and I had my lessons from the piano teacher, and I could sit down and practice until -- just take time out to eat, and go right back to the piano. The piano began to fascinate me. Because it had so much more scope than a guitar, you know. As great as a guitar -- it's a great instrument to listen to, but the piano itself, it's a big instrument, you know. It can teach you to write. It'll teach you a whole lot of things if you go about it in the proper way, you know. But with supervision. Don't jump over the fence before you know what's going to happen. So --
Do you remember the name of your first piano teacher?

It was a lady, but I remember the guy that carried me down the road. His name was Josephus Robinson. A very good classical man. And oh, we used to have like church concerts and I used to have to go down and play some Mendelssohn and play a little Bach, you know, and I was so nervous I didn't know what I was doing. It turned out all right, you know, I just didn't want to disappoint my parents at that time. And they were pretty proud that their efforts were paying off.
Well, Mr. Robinson came after your earlier teacher, is that right?
Well, that was one, I can't remember her name, but she was a lady.
Uh-huh.

And -- oh, I have a funny thing to tell you. I'd come in the house and I'd start playing. I had my lessons, you know, and I'd start playing things like, maybe, 'Honeysuckle Rose,' or something, doing that by ear, and then she would have the lessons, you know, for me to learn.
Uh-huh.

And I got to the point where I could play the lessons by ear, I'd play them all by ear, you know? Memorize them. And she just -- one day she said, 'Well, James, you did so well on that one, let's turn the page and go to the next one.'
(Laughter)

I never tried that anymore. Said no, no, that's not going to work anymore, you know. But she was a good teacher, a very good teacher. And then things went on, and after I got into high school I started playing bass, bass violin, you know.
How did you happen to take up bass, too?
It was there. This was a fine high school
in Chicago.
What high school?
Englewood. Englewood High School. It was one of the biggest at that time. And you learned orchestral instruments. And then you'd take up organ. Not electric organ, but the big one.
Pipe organ?
Yeah, pipe organ, yeah.
They had a pipe organ in the high school?

Oh, yeah. Well, the building was four stories high, you know, and all of the bottom notes, the lower manual, you could play it so softly, you could shake the building. It was a building that housed 6,000 students, you know. And it was very well put together, you know. It had good teachers and they are quite important to me now. I don't know where all of them are today, but they are -- they were very thorough in their work. And I was taking physics, chemistry, botany, zoology and two years of Latin. I wanted to be a doctor.
Oh.

That was my first love, you know. Professionally, you know, to be my first love. But as the Depression began to hit the music took over because that was a thing right at my fingertips to make some money. Then I got
into that and had to stay in it. I was locked into it. I had to stay there, you know.
You know, there seems to be quite a few people who have been interested in both music and medicine. Is there some kind of correlation between music and medicine?
There seems to be.
What is it?

We don't know, because there was a big article in the New York Times some years ago that said -- it says wherever you find like a doctor -- like the statement is you speak of today, you find another person inside of yourself, you know? Wherever you find a doctor there's a musician.
I know a lot of doctors play.
Love -- but they love musicians.
Well, there's a doctors' symphony here in Los Angeles, isn't there?

Yeah. It's quite an association, and I asked the late Arthur Logan, Ellington's doctor, you know, I said, 'Why?' And he gave me I guess possibly the most logical answer. He says, 'When you've got --,' especially jazz. He says, 'All of you guys can play the blues, but it's the matter of the man that takes the best solo.' And he says, 'Well, okay. We all read X-rays, and if a person needs surgery it's the man
that takes the best solo on surgery." And I said, "Well, gee, that's a great parallel."
But you're improvising on your solo, usually. You're not improvising exactly in surgery, are you?

Yeah, well -- he told me sometimes the X-rays don't tell them all, and they go, when they go inside with a patient, and the guy that's got the talent to do it is the one that makes the patient survive. I says, "Oh, is that the reason, Doc?"
(Laughter)
So I became one of his patients, you know. But that was the best explanation I've heard.
Uh-huh. That's very interesting.
Where I could relate to it myself, you know?
So when you were playing bass, were you playing both piano and bass, or did you just concentrate on the bass?
No, the bass belonged to the Chicago school system, and when I went to junior college in Chicago, Wilson Junior College, they had a little symphony band there, you know?
Uh-huh.
And I would play bass in the symphony band. We'd do, "The Bohemian Girl," and, "La Boheme," and a
lot of things, you know? And then playing piano, you know, gigging at the same time. And just try -- well, we were all trying to make ends meet. See, Marty Young, Joe Williams.
He wasn't Joe Williams yet, was he? Didn't he have -- wasn't his last name something else?
Yeah. It started with a G.
I can't remember what it is, but I think it's in the encyclopedia.
Yeah. It started with a G. Goreed (PHONETIC).
Yeah.
In fact he was the first one to sign my graduation annual, the year book, when you graduate from high school or something, you know?
You and Joe went to high school together?

Yeah, we went to high school together and we used to live next door to each other, when we were both about 15 years old, because I think -- Joe just had his birthday. We're the same age, only two weeks apart.
Yeah, and Joe's two weeks older than you, right?
Yeah.
That's right, Joe's birthday was last week.
Yeah, so -- and we just never knew that this thing -- as far as our partnership, musically, was going to develop this way.
It's a long association.
Yeah, we used to --
From 15 year olds to 'The Tonight Show' now.
Yeah. Now we're pushing 1980.
(Laughter)
Marl Morrow was in high school with you too?

Yes. Marl Morrow Young. I met Marl Morrow Young in -- it was 1932, when I first came out of grammar school. And then we both went through -- we both graduated and went to Wilson Junior College and we've been knowing each other for -- you know, since I was wearing knickers.
Was Marl Morrow playing then too?
Uh-huh. In fact I took piano lessons from Marl Morrow.
Oh. Well, Marl Morrow had, what started earlier than you? Are you and Marl Morrow the same age?

No, I think he's a bit older than I am, but I just liked the way -- my habit is always to be around contemporary people as teachers, not so much the older people. And that -- I think that -- I still do. Even in the writing
and the studying, the things that I want to do today, I want to be around the guys my age or younger.
Uh-huh.

You know, because it keeps me going. I can get a rapport with them or something, you know. So Marj Morrow and I, we came up together, and he went to John Marshall Law School, and I went to Kentucky State University, and I got involved with sociology, you know?
How did you happen to decide to major in sociology?

Well, I had no idea what I wanted to major in. But going into the registrar's office, and just write down something. I should have had some advice, but I just said sociology because it seemed popular.
(Laughter)
I must have been nuts. 17, 18 years old, you know. But after I got into it I liked it. And even Whitney Young was there. He was right in the line with me. You know?
Did he major in sociology because it was popular too?

Yeah, he was in -- I think he was in sociology. I think so. I'm not sure, because we all stayed in the dormitory, you know. One thing I remember, after I'd been to Englewood High School and had had physics and chemistry and all that, I used to go and help -- excuse me --

Whitney with his physical science. See by that time they'd begun to combine the classes. It was physical science. But when I was going to school you took botany was one course, and zoology was another course, so you were thoroughly educated on it, you know? Whitney and I stayed quite a bit in touch until his death, you know? We felt a little proud of each other after leaving the campus.
Of course.
You know, we went out and tried to do something about ourselves, you know?
Were you the only child in your family or did you have any brothers and sisters?

Well, I had two sisters, they were twins, and a brother, but they were all still births. I was the only one that lived, you know? And oh, I wish they were around now, you know? You know, after -- I think that's one of the reasons all the concentration came on me.
Oh, of course, that would make sense, sure.
You know? They weren't hard on me or anything like that, but they would always direct me. Oh, I'm going to tell a little funny story. I guess it's about time for that, maybe.
Okay.
I was about third year high school, and
you know how a buy begins to walk the girls home carry their books for them and all that?
Uh-huh.

So for me to walk this little girl home, I would always have to pass by -- there was no way to get to her house but to pass by my house, and my mother would always sit in the front window. She knew exactly what time I was supposed to be there, which hour. And they sat me down, my father and mother sat me down at dinner, and they said one thing that has stuck. He says, "James, before you make us a family, finish school so you can support them." And you know, I've been reading ever since. That thing caught on to me, you know? I said I'd better be qualified here before I take on responsibilities, you know?
Good advice.
Yeah. Well, at least my head was spongey, then.

This is December 23rd, and we're continuing the interview with Jimmy Jones, and right after we left off before you said that you wanted to talk about John Collins when we resumed. You said that he had something to do with your not continuing guitar.
Yes. In that the first time I heard John Collins I was with the singing trio, and I was a little

guitar player. We were all influenced by the Mills Brothers in those days. And I heard this man play guitar, and -- oh, now and then I'll pick it up, but after that it stayed in the corner. I said, 'Well, I can't go in that direction, because this man is a master, and he still is a master of his instrument.' Master teacher and everything. He's got the knowledge and -- a complete professional.
At that time, when you first knew John, was he working professionally already?
Yes. He was working with -- was it Dan Grissom (UNINTELLIGIBLE)? It was a trio. Yeah, it was a trio on 47th Street in Chicago. You remember Dan Grissom, the vocalist with Jimmy Lunceford?
Yeah.
And his mother played piano.
John's mother.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.

And we came in just to make a performance. We were making a little noise in the neighborhood as singers. And I played my little -- it was really a four stringed guitar. Later on I learned the six stringed guitar, you know. But then I heard John Collins and I just said, 'Well, I cannot go in that direction.'
All right. We had a little interruption there. One thing I wanted to ask you before you go on, and that

Let's see. There was -- one of the fellow you possibly might have met over at Bob Singleton's house, a tall fellow named Eddie Johnson, and if your remember Mari Morrow Young was speaking about Eddie Johnson, as we all went to school. We all went to junior college together, you know? And Eddie was right there on the lawn, too, you know?
Over at Bob Singleton's house. That was the day that you were honored by the Jazz Heritage Foundation a few months weeks ago.
Yeah.
Yeah.

So he was just out here with his wife on a visit, and it was a beautiful weekend, you know, because we go back. I think Eddie was 13 when I first met him. Yes, as I was speaking about Eddie, but later on he was taking classical piano in The Loop, during the time when I was going through my different things with guitar and piano around the house, and then Eddie switched over to saxophone. And became a very dominant tenor saxophone player. In fact he was the one that was scouted to take Ben Webster's place with Ellington's band, before Skippy Williams. He was the man, you know? And --
Is he still playing?
Yes. Well he's very interested in flute now, because he and Jerome Richardson got together.
Uh-huh.
You know, at Bob's house.
Uh-huh.
And he's highly interested in -- he's not in the music business as of now. He's in another profession that has lasted very well for him.
What is it that he does now?
What the heck does he do? I don't know. But it's high level work, you know?
Uh-huh.

Because that seemed to be the thing around Chicago in those days, because it didn't have the thing that New York had at that time. You had to leave Chicago if you were going to be in this business that I'm in. So the guys would end up buying property and going into real estate and playing music on the side, you know? That was the -- those were the social overtones there, then, at that time.
It wasn't possible to earn a good living in music in Chicago.

No. You could -- if you were young, you could get around a little bit, you know, but as time went, especially if a man had a family, and responsibilities, the best thing for him to do was just to get into something which is seemingly more stable, you know? But I was just possibly very fortunate when I went to New York, and had no idea what was
going to happen. I didn't -- I kept my keys at home with my mother's sister, my aunt, in case I had to come back, you know. You don't know how you're going to turn out, you know.
Who was the other member of the trio besides you and Eddie?

His name was Leroy Winbush (MONROE). Oh, I guess he's got his first dollar. He's very wealthy today. He went into commercial art, like E. Simmons [Easoms] Campbell, and he has all the accounts, the banks and things in the Loop in Chicago.
Was [Easoms] Campbell from Chicago?
No, not [Easoms] Campbell. What I was speaking of --
That kind of artwork?
That kind of work.
I see. Yes.

And Eddie told me a thing that -- when he was here -- that he had a thing to go to Singapore with the Chinese government, and Roy was always smart in that direction, you know. Even when he was about 17 and we were together, you know? And he made quite a success of himself, and he's got a good business head, and straight ahead, and his feet are still on the ground. In fact, Eddie was trying to get me to get a picture of us, because Roy wanted it, to use it for a TV show that they might make a special, on him. You know? Because
he's a quiet man.
Do you still have the picture?

Couldn't find it. Looked for it and couldn't find it. Now, I have another one, but I think Roy wanted the one that -- I know the one that Roy wanted. Oh, let's see, we were about -- Roy was 17, I was 15 and Eddie was 13. And we were just kids, you know?
Uh-huh. How long did you keep the trio together?
Oh, let me see. Quite a few years. Oh, maybe three or four. That was a long time to us in those days, you know?
Sure. Well, to teenagers it is.
Yeah. And we didn't quite realize what we had at that time. We just were doing like a neighborhood thing, you know, having a good time and playing at little parties.
What was the name of the club that John was working in?
Oh, John Collins.
Yeah, uh-huh. When you said that --
Doc Huggins'.
Uh-huh.
And this same trio came in, we came in to perform, and you know, because as I was saying we made a little
noise and John Collins was playing there with his mother, you know, as I said before.
Uh-huh.
And Dan Grissom. All three of us in the trio played guitar, but I turned out to be a chief guitar player, if you want to put it that way.
(Laughter)
And he said, 'Well, now, Jim, you play guitar and pass out the singing notes.' So I would rehearse everybody. But I was the only one that sang out of tune.
(Laughter)
Everybody else could sing, you know. Roy was a little slow on getting his part, but when he got it you couldn't move him.
Do you think -- is there any relation to being able to sing in and out of tune and a person's ability on an instrument, or a person's ear?

I think that's what got in my way, because when I was a kid and didn't have to play I used to go around and -- this was before my voice broke -- singing at church concerts in Chicago. And then, when I graduated from grammar school, I was the soloist, you know, like you see at choirs in churches?
Uh-huh.
I was a soloist. But I didn't -- my voice

was real high then. And the only thing -- the reason I was singing out of tune later is I was concentrating on the sound of the whole group and the guitar, so I wasn't thinking about my own pitch, you know?
Uh-huh.
And that's -- that's how that thing came about, you know. I had no idea that I would get that involved with music. As I told you, I liked medicine first.
Uh-huh.
Even when I was in grammar school, my ambition was to be a doctor. It just took money to go to med school, you know, and we didn't have it. It was that simple, you know?
Well, did you get around as a teenager to hear much music in Chicago? Were you aware of who all was playing while you were in your teens?

Well, not so -- yes, I did, by record. There were disc jockeys there. There was one named Bob Hawk. I don't know whether he's around now or not, and he used to play Ellington quite a bit. And he played Lunceford. And there was a fellow that played piano. His name was Dick Baker, Two Ton Baker.
Oh, sure.
And he could play Ellington on piano, I mean play the arrangements on piano.
I've heard him play, yes.

All the people -- yeah, uh-huh.

And we -- out of all those groups there Leonard talked RCA Victor into doing it. And I'm really glad he did. We had no idea what we were doing. We didn't know it was anything going to be that historical.
Yeah, you don't know at the time.

Yeah. You know, you just go and do it. You just make the record date and make the job and take the money and run, you know? Then, as years go by you realize what you've done. I told someone the other day, I said, 'Gee, whiz, I've been lucky enough to get these accolades in this late stage in my career, but had I thought about it this way I wouldn't have done it that way. I would have started making targets for myself, things to cover, you know?'
Do you think it would have worked better that way, Jimmy?
Uh-uh.
I don't either. I think the --
Just do the job. I was just so interested in the music, and getting that done, and I had no idea that these pleasant side effects were going to happen.
Uh-huh.

I had no idea, you know. In fact, I still don't. A lot of people say, "You're too modest." I'm not modest. It's just that music is bigger than I am. You know. It's just like trying to breathe in all the fresh air and reap all the sunshine. It's a great art, you know? Now that's the way I think of it. And I'm so happy that I'm making a living at something that would have been a hobby anyway.
Yeah.
I'm one of the fortunate few.
Well, you also have an exceptional talent.
Well, there are a whole lot of guys that are talented. They just weren't standing on the right corner at the right time. When the right person came around.
Doing the right thing.
Yeah.
I'll remember that. Now, you do something very special that there's nobody else does it quite like you do. And that's why you're where you are and who you are.
Pat, do you know that to me -- I don't know, let's see. To me it's just --

When you sit down at the piano some very beautiful things come out and they're unique. Nobody else plays them. They don't occur to anybody else. I mean have you listened to your, "Orson," on Ellington's record.
Yeah, I liked it.
You'd better.

Yeah, I did. Because a lot of times I do things that I'm not -- I say, "Gee, I could have done this that way or this way." You know. You hear -- you always hear something else you might have done, in retrospect, you know. But I liked it. I sat there last night and just put it on and I put it on where it would repeat that whole last side, starting with -- that's a good album.
It sure is a good album.
You know, I listened to the whole thing. That's a good album. I think I like some of the things in this one better than I do the last one.
Well, they're both good.
Yeah.
But there are some very exciting things happening here.
Because I talked with Kenny about it, you know, and I said, "Kenny how does it sound?" I'm more
interested in how the music sounds. How did it come off? He says it's good, man. Just like that.
Yeah, Kenny was very happy with it.
Yeah. Well, we had so much stored up. From the first album, that we could always use it for the second one.
Yeah. It was such good things. I mean we only intended to do enough material for one album the first time, but there was nothing that could be discarded out of it.
No, there was too many great musicians and too much -- I guess it was just that the chemistry was there. And I have to agree with you.
Plus we had the beauty of having Butter with us the second time.
Oh, yes. Yes. That's -- that was -- Kenny and I talked about that, too. To let him sing -- and he was a good singer.
Yes, he was. You know, he was so thrilled. Remember how excited he was that Kenny wanted him to sing and Kenny liked what he did?
Yeah.
And they were talking about doing an album, but Kenny wanted to produce an album of Butter singing.
Yeah.
And Butter was so happy. And Kenny would have done it, you know, had there been time.

Yeah. But I had no idea, you know, that Butter -- I knew his health had been shaky, but I had no idea that -- because he just didn't seem like it, as he was telling those stories when we went out to dinner?
Yeah. No, he seemed in fine spirits, like he felt good, and I think he did feel good then.

Yeah. And when Jerome Richardson called me up and said, "I've got some news," you know, and I didn't know what it was, you know. I thought maybe something might have happened to Quincy again. And he said, "No, this time it's Buddy. He's gone." You know, I guess he probably had one of those coronaries or something.
Yeah. They say right while he was playing in the pit. He was doing a show. He was doing, I think -- was it "Guys and Dolls?"
Yeah.
It happened during the show.
You know, we had a -- when we were -- we were staying at the Marriott.
Uh-huh.
Butter and I would talk about different foods to eat. And he was saying his wife, to keep him off of
pork and different, you know, things that were negative to his system, she knew how to cook corn, but you know he was basically still pretty stout.
Yeah. But he'd lost a lot of weight. He had to. They ordered him to.
Well, yes, he was pretty big before then, you know?
Yeah.
So -- but you know he had such a wealth -- now there's a guy I would like to have seen you work with on a book.

Well, Butter and I were talking about it. You know, he did an oral history for the Smithsonian. And I said, 'I'm sure glad they did that, Butter, because otherwise I was going to get to you and you and I were going to sit down with a tape recorder.' He said, 'Oh, we can still do that, Pat. I only gave them five hours.'
(Laughter)
Oh, yeah, because he could talk -- this guy had so much experience and so much background, you know?
Yeah.
And he could have talked for days, five days on it.
I know. Jimmy Knepper Nefford (PHONETIC) told me that. He said -- and Butter and I of course had been friends

since way back in Duke's band. But Jimmy said that when he was on the road with Thad's band, he said that that's what they used to do nights on the road, is everybody gather around Butter and Butter would sit and tell stories, and he said nobody would sleep. They would sit up all night because Butter had so many fascinating stories to tell.
Yeah.
And he said he didn't retell anything. Every night there was a whole set of new experiences that Butter would talk about.
Yeah. Yeah. A man of deep experience, you know?
Uh-huh.
And he retained it. That's --
Yeah. All of it.
-- the beauty of it, you know? Now, he's gone back to Fletcher Henderson. He's gone way back.
Yeah.
I don't mean the '30s for Fletcher Henderson. I mean the early Fletcher Henderson.
Yeah, well he went -- McKinley's Cotton Pickers he started with.
Yeah, that's right. That goes back further, you know?
Uh-huh.
And he could still play. He never lost it.
Uh-uh.
See, that's that thing we were speaking about a little while ago, back on the tape, you know? There's something about music, once you have it and if you're born to do it you don't lose it. You know?
Uh-huh.
You know, barring bad health or something like that, you know. As we've noticed with Eubie Blake. That's a crowning example.
He's marvelous.
Yeah. He's -- this guy, his hands are just as flexible and all that, you know, just -- like I said, his knees and his legs, but if you stand on your legs 95 years something's got to give, you know?
Right.
Yeah.
Well, his hands are amazing. He has the longest fingers I've ever seen.
Yeah.
It's fascinating to watch -- when we were over at your friend's house, you know, that day?
Yeah.
And getting to stand right up next
to the piano while he played was a treat. It was intriguing to watch his hands move. Not just to listen, you know, but to see what happened.
You should have seen him conduct. He gave me my first conducting lesson.
How old were you?
Oh, by that time I was -- oh, let's see, I was -- I was married and everything by then.
How old were you when you got married?
Let me see. Baby, I'll get this together in a minute.
I'll bet Speedy would have remembered.
Oh, yeah. We got married in '45. That's right, because Eubie and Marion got married in '46, a year later. We both -- all of us were living in Brooklyn then, you know?
Uh-huh.
And Eubie was going to -- 1945, I should have been -- well, you can figure it out. Look in Leonard's book.
Let's see, you were born in 1918.
Yeah.
All right.
The end of 1918.
The tail end. The last couple of days.
Yeah.
Okay.
Because I'm trying to -- I'm trying to bring 1919 in, but it ain't going to work.
(Laughter)
Yeah, you see, you can get it from there. And I think I met Eubie the next year, '46. I was working at Cafe Society with J. C. Heard (PHONETIC), and that's when I first met Sarah. And --
You were working with J. C. Heard and whom?

Let's see, I'll tell you who was in the band. Budd Johnson. Well, J. C. McKibbon Al McGiven (PHONETIC). Dickie Wells and George Joyce Treadwell. It was a nice little group, you know? And Eubie was -- he took -- I think he went to NYU before I did, and studied with Rudolph Schramm, the great Schillinger teacher, you know?
Uh-huh.

And let's see, I've got to write Schramm, because I don't think he knows Speedy's Sweetie's gone. We used to hang out together, you know? There was a funny thing, you know, when I used to buy these textbooks, and I would conduct very stiff, and Eubie had a nine foot grand at his house. So we just took the "Star Spangled Banner," you see. Okay, give me
the "Star Spangled Banner," and I was conducting -- just like that. Square, you know. Right angles.
With a clenched fist?
No, no, no, no, no.
Okay.
And Eubie played it like that. I said, "Eubie, what's wrong?" He said, "That's the way you conducted me." Then he got up and his hands were very fluid and -- you know?
Uh-huh.

Very easy. Because he'd had all that experience in the pit, you know, conducting shows on Broadway, uptown, so it was -- as of now they have him as a ragtime piano player, but he's a well rounded musician, well rounded. But he just happens to be a very funny man, a great sense of humor.
He certainly does, from what I've seen of him in television interviews, and then that day we spent an hour at his house.
Oh, he's going to be funny. And he's not trying to be. He's just born that way.
Well, he's got a sense of humor, though. I mean he knows he's being funny. It's not an unconscious thing.
No, he knows he's -- well, he loves an
audience, you know.
Obviously.

All of us hams love an audience, you know? I'd like -- when I get on stage or playing or something, you -- I like it. Especially when the audience likes it. I feel like a million dollars when the audience likes it, you know, because if I fell in love with what I played I'd be nuts. But --
Back to Chicago. Where did you work with the Stuff Smith Trio? Do you remember the clubs?

Yeah. The Three Deuces, which was in the Loop, on Wabash Avenue, and the Garrick Lounge, which was on Randolph. And the Garrick Lounge was a very special kind of a place. It was an upstairs and a downstairs. I worked with Red Allen in the Garrick Lounge too. With Higginbottom (PHO1 ham NETC). Yeah, that group. Well, at that point Stuff wouldn't go to the Garrick Lounge, so Red Allen came to my house because he liked the way I played. I said, "Well, Stuff, if you're not going over to the Garrick, I'm going." And the guy at the Garrick that owned it, Joe Sherman, wanted Stuff there. But Stuff just was getting complacent where he was, you know? I says, "Stuff, I'm going to leave you." And then Stuff came and I joined Stuff. Red was still working in the club. So I just went right from Red back to Stuff. And, let's see, Pete Brown was working upstairs. Let's see, Ray Nance wasn't there. I don't know if Ray -- Ray Nance -- I don't know whether Ray
Nance was giggin around the Garrick Lounge or not, because he was still with Duke at that point.
But you knew Ray before he went with Duke, didn't you? Or did you know of him?

I knew him, yeah. But I -- you know, in those days Ray Nance was one of the Chicago stars, if you want to put it that way. Even though he didn't act like it. He was never arrogant. But Ray was one of the -- he had one of the nicest little six pieces, you know. All three of them in the front line played violin.
Oh.
They doubled. Just like he did, you know?
Oh, I didn't realize what the instrumentation was. I knew he had a group. Didn't he start it when he was still in high school?
Yeah. They were very early.
Yeah.
And I used to see some church programs where they would say Raymond Nance on violin. And he would play like church affairs and things like that.
Do you know who the musicians were that were in the front line in his band?
Oh, boy, let me see. John Levy would know. I know Spencer Odum (PHONETIC), who's passed, too. Used to play with the Southernairs, the quartet that used to come
on in DC every Sunday.
Uh-huh.
And -- now I can't think of the rest of them, but John Levy would know, because he was coming along at that time, too, you know?
When you left Stuff and went back to him, did John stay with him all that time? Was John with him then? He must have been, because you said John got you with Stuff.
Yeah. Oh, yes. Yes.
John stayed with him.
Yes. Now we're going back to Chicago now.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Yeah. Yeah, but --
Something else I'm curious about are those big bands you mentioned. You said Nat had a big band. Do you know who was in that? Can you remember?
No. I was --
You were playing --
I wasn't dry behind the ears at that time. I was just -- I was really --
Because you said you played in Hambo's band and --
[Fambro] (PHONETIC).
[Fambro] yeah, excuse me.
Yeah.
And you had the battle of the bands.
Yeah, but at that time they had stopped having those battles of the bands. I joined [Fambro] (PHONETIC) after that, but I used to be around -- hang around the bandstand to listen to them.
Oh, I see.

And they used to call [Fambro] "Little Duke", because they had some trumpet players that could growl like Cootie and you know, in those days. And it was a Duke Ellington orientated thing. But Nat Cole was a completely different thing. You know?
In what way?
The musical sound was different. It was a regular big band sound, you know?
Did Nat write for the band?
I don't know whether he wrote then or not, but I know he did a lot of writing later.
I know he did too, but I just wondered if he had then for that band.
Because he had -- he was -- he had so much taste about what he was doing musically, you know?
Uh-huh.
And -- but these -- the only thing about Tony [Fambro] -- and we had some good musicians. Oh, yeah, because two of the guys, gee whiz, Duke used to steal men out of [Fambro's] band.
Who did he steal?
One was called Sax Mallard.
Uh-huh.
He was playing alto and another one was called Nat Jones.
Uh-huh.
You know? And they were in the band. We only had those eight pieces, but you know --
What did Nat Jones play?

Nat Jones played clarinet just like Barney Bigard, and alto -- I can't describe the style. It was different, a very interesting thing. It caught Duke's ear. And he went out with Duke for a while, you know. But they didn't like that road.
Yeah, it was rough.

You know? They just didn't like that road. And they all went back -- they all went back home. They're doing well. Nat's got a lot of real estate and stuff, you know. He doesn't have to break his neck anymore. And they just play for fun, you know. Fine musicians. Just like the same situation I was speaking of -- the socio-economic thing

of Chicago. You know, the situation just sends you somewhere else, no matter what you started out to do. For survival you just have to adjust, you know. You have to keep your head above water, you know. And there's another thing, where drifting towards an Ellington type sound, because all of us admired the Ellington band. At that time, you know. We loved that band, you know? All the musicians loved it. And I think I was on my way, maybe simply because -- maybe that was one of the reasons I was with Tony [Fambro,] because -- well, it leaned towards Ellington, you know.
Do you remember who else was in the band?

Well, John Levy was playing bass in it. And then there was a fellow named Pete Smith playing drums, and the growl trumpet player's name was Russell Gillam (PHONETIC). That's the one I told you about when we were stranded, helped to do the cooking with John Levy.
Was that the Indianapolis stranding?
Yeah. There wasn't nothing but beans and rice, but it filled us up, you know. And who else? Well, Nat Jones and Sax Mallard. Until Duke started robbing Fambro of his men.
He did that to a few bands didn't he?
Yes, he did. He started robbing them. And -- but they didn't stick, you know. But --
When you were working at the Garrick and at the Two Deuces, who else was working around Chicago? What other music was being --
Well, right around the corner, let's see, Eddie South, Billy Taylor, and I can't remember who was on bass. It was really swinging in those days, you know?
Billy Taylor the bass player or Billy Taylor the piano player?

No, no, the piano player. Uh-huh. Let's see. I think I mentioned Pete Brown working in the Garrick Lounge upstairs. It was something. The Garrick was laid out something like the -- what's that club on Seventh Avenue in New York, across the street from the Copper Rail?
Oh, the Metropole?
The Metropole, yeah. Day and night.
Uh-huh.

Yeah. This was upstairs and downstairs. And -- I can't remember, but I remember times when the Budapest Quartet used to come there to hear Stuff. Because he had something going. He was a tough man on his instrument, you know?
Uh-huh.
I don't think he ever got his due credit, but I don't think he allowed himself to get it. He would go off and chase ladies and wouldn't settle down completely to his
business.
Were there more jazz violin players in Chicago than anyplace else? I mean what -- Eddie South of course was more than just jazz. He played --
Gypsy. You know, more legitimate, really.

Yeah. But him, Ray Nance, Stuff, and then you talk about Ray having three violins in the front line. It sounds like there was a big concentration of jazz violinists. Moreso than any other city, wasn't there?
Well, coming up, when I was coming along, you either had a piano in your home or your parents would send you to a violin teacher.
It was the popularity of the instrument itself in the era.

Yeah. That was the thing to do at that time. You know, and you'd play in church. And the parents would like to show their children off, just like when I played the -- started playing some classical concerts, my piano teacher would give me -- Mr. Robinson, he would give concerts in the churches. That was our biggest social contact with everybody else, you know?
Well, life sort of revolved around what happened in the church.
Yes. So at -- that just happened to happen at that time. And I don't know. It was -- that was a good

question, because you know I never thought about that. Like when you were speaking about Ray Nance and the guys in his front line. His band was six pieces. But I forget who was in it. Something like John Kirby. Had they gotten out of Chicago and gotten to New York, they would have made it. Very unique, you know? Excuse me. But it just broke up and then pretty soon Ray wound up with Duke. And he evidently loved it, because he stayed there a long time, you know?
Yeah, he loved Duke. He called him his musical father and --
The guys really down deep in their hearts, they loved the old man.
Well, some more than others. I think Ray for instance more than some of the others.
Yes.
I mean Ray knew and had recognized and come up against the other side of Duke, but he still loved him very much.
Yeah. And I saw the other side of him, but I still loved him, you know? He had something.
He sure did.
I don't know what it was, but he had something.
Well, there was just no place in life you could find the Ellington experience except right there
with Duke.
Yeah.
He wasn't like anybody else.
No.
Anywhere, ever, before or since.

No, no, not at all. Because his music was -- it was the same thing, different. Completely different. He had another kind of an imagination, you know? Oh, getting back to him, what I -- I'm trying to pull these things together. Fambro and the other guys, after we'd been together for awhile, and then I worked with another band called Danny Williams. It was a local band in Chicago. Didn't have the same thing that I wanted to associate with that Tony Fambro had, you know? And that's the band that I went to Kentucky State with, because they wanted to get the collegians, you know, and that's how we were earning our way through school, like football players.
Well, which came first, Tony[Fambro's] band went to --
Yes.
That's the band that went to Kentucky State?
No, no, no.
The Williams band.
Danny Williams' band.
Went to --
Kentucky State, yeah.
And became the Collegians.
Yeah.
I thought you were already going there and got involved in the Collegians. The Collegians went there. The band --

Yeah. They imported the band from Chicago, an organized band, and there was a social science teacher, Arnold Wright, who was like a second father to me. He had a lot to do with the Alabama State Collegians, with the -- what's his name? Erskine Hawkins.
Uh-huh.
Then he started teaching on the Kentucky State campus and found out there was another way to take advantage of getting some money in and give some guys some education.
How nice.
You know? And it worked. It really worked. And as that letter says that you're reading, now this is going back at -- to 1940. Gee whiz.
That's when you went to Kentucky State, was --
Yeah, just about '40, I think. But see,

the -- no, no, no. Before then. What the heck am I thinking about. Because I was just about a junior there and the war, in '41, when we had the Pearl Harbor thing, they dissolved it. A lot of the football players even were drafted, you know. They had to dissolve a lot of programs, you know. So I came back to Chicago.
So how long were you at Kentucky State?

I was at Wilson for about -- the junior college that I mentioned before -- about a year, little more than a year. It wasn't nothing but just a two year education, but I went to Kentucky State for about two and a half years. I only needed about 30 hours for a bachelors, and what I was going after, you know? But they just dissolved everything and I didn't have any money, so I had to get back to Chicago.
But it was during that period at Kentucky State that you wrote the school song, is that right?
Yeah.
Had you -- was that the first time you'd done any writing? You hadn't mentioned any writing. When was the first time you started writing?
I'm going to start this with a joke.
All right.
And I wrote it for Danny Williams's band. This was after I left [Fambro.] The first arrangement I ever wrote or attempted, it felt like it took me a year, was, "East
St. Louis Toodledoo."
Oh, who did you write that for, the Danny Williams band?
Uh-huh, because he had a big band, see. Tony only had eight pieces.
Uh-huh.
But he was more associated with Duke. But there were more horns with Danny Williams, you know?
How many pieces all together?

Five brass. At that time that was a big band. Five brass and four reeds. Was it four reeds? I guess it was four reeds and the regular rhythm section. You know? And my father used to look at me, he'd say, "James, I sure hope you finish that arrangement, because you've been banging on the piano all night and all day, trying to get yourself together." You know, he didn't use those words. And my mother had just died a little before then, you know, and so the old man and I, we had an apartment together, a small apartment. And the only therapy -- the best therapy I had was that music. Because I was in shock. He was, too. But by him being a choir director and fiddle player and whatever, that got him off the ground.
Uh-huh.
So he could last, you know? Because they stayed together like that, you know.
So while you were at Kentucky State
your father was with you?
Yeah, he was still alive then.
Yeah, but I mean he was in Kentucky?
No, no. He -- we went down there together. He met Mr. Wright on the campus, the Mr. Wright I was telling you about, you know?
Uh-huh.

And we had struggled up on an Oldsmobile, and the old man came down with me to talk with the teachers, you know, meet them and let them know that he was interested in how I was going to come along, you know, and he stayed in the dormitory with us, and he drove on back to Chicago, you know? And I stayed there. It was a great experience.
Oh, I'm sure. Well, I guess, 'East St. Louis Toodledoo,' must have been a success, because you went on to write the school song. Was it right after that?
We used to play this song with Tony Fambro.
Oh.
Before.
Oh, and then it sort of got moved on over to be the school song.
Yeah. I wrote it down there at the campus, you know. And they're still using it, you know.
The name of the school song is what?
It's called, "Dog, Cat and Me."

Oh. They didn't really say that here. They said, "At present we've been unable to locate any examples of the types of music played by the Collegians. An example of that would be, "Dog Cat and Me," the theme song of the Collegians. If you have any musical scores or could notate some of this for us, it would be very helpful." But it doesn't even sound for sure as though they're aware that you wrote that. They only know that you were a member of the Collegians. This is a letter that you got from Kentucky State University about two years ago, right?
Yeah.
In which they're trying trace down information --
Trying to get to it.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Who the personnel of the band was and all about it. Can you remember who all was in the band?
No. Well -- we were all just about amateurs in a way. I guess I was the only one that had a little professional experience, as I was saying, out of necessity.
Danny Williams didn't have any exprience?
Yeah, he played like dances around

Chicago, things like that. And they had a lot of -- they had a thing where they would have social clubs in high schools, you know, something like fraternities and sororities and that kind of thing going, you know?
Uh-huh.

But other than that, I mean the real hard experience. And when I -- let's see, I was still working with John Levy and Tony [Fambro,] and -- now let me try to tie this together. No, then they didn't have it. Oh, yeah, now. Some of the guys -- all of them didn't stay there. They -- a lot of them drifted back to Chicago, you know. But I liked the campus. I liked that life, you know? And I made a lot of friends there. So I stayed on. And the guys that came in were like people from the State of Kentucky. They could play pretty fair instruments, you know.
Uh-huh.
But not really as good as the guys that left to go back to Chicago.
Did Danny Williams stay?
No, he didn't stay.
What instrument did he play?

Saxophone. He didn't have to stay, because he was well off. His people had property, and they were from the Williams Singers, at the turn of the century were very famous, you know. That was his mother and father, you know.
Oh.
And they'd been to Europe and performed for state heads and everything, you know. But when I got down to Kentucky I wrote, 'Dog, Cat and Me.'
For the band.
Yeah.
And then it got picked up as the school song?
Yeh. It's just --
And you told me I believe recently that it is still the school song, right?
Yeah. I think so, because -- well when I got there I was going through a crisis and my head wasn't completely clear. But --
You're talking about when you received the letter, that was right about the time your wife died.
Yes. And I didn't have the energy to do this at that time. I had to work myself out of what I was into. I really haven't read this thing thoroughly.

Well, it says they're doing some research. They're trying to -- there's a professor there who has a research project who's trying to find out as much as he can about the Collegians, because they say they feel that it was a very significant musical group.
Yeah, well, we did have a nice group. We developed into one, because the guys stayed in school. A
lot of them became doctors and lawyers, very successful in other areas, you know. But they played in the band to get through school.
That's very interesting.
You know?
Like the kinds of -- today, athletic scholarships. But is there anyplace that has scholarships like this? Well, maybe a music school.
Alabama State and Maryland State. All of those eastern southern states or colleges that were basically black, even though they had some white students too, but they had those setups.
Where you could earn your way through on a music scholarship.
Yeah.
In order to have a good band.
Yeah.
That's great.
And it was one of the finest experiences that I have ever had, because it really rounded me out.
You mentioned early, when we first started to talk, about when you went back with your father when -- was it Le Moine University honored him?
Oh, yes.
And you said that it was integrated there. Did you mean at the university or did you mean in the
Yeah, at the university.
Oh. It was completely integrated or --
Uh-huh.
And that would have been, well you said you were about eight or nine years old.

Uh-huh. Because all the homes we went to were -- not all of them, but they respected my father highly. And these were white homes. There was no problem, no nothing. We had a ball, you know? It was no -- nothing like what came up later. Now they say it's really improved greatly. Like at Fisk University, we used to play -- what we would play was -- like with the Collegians, we travelled to all the schools. West Virginia State, Fisk University, and the University of Kentucky. Playing homecomings.
Uh-huh.

You just remembered your uncle's name, I think, right?
Yeah. Benjamin Young. And he got to be

great friends with James Petrillo because Petrillo was the President of the Federation at that time. And that was just before the recording strike, and my uncle kept warning me to watch out for it, because Petrillo didn't like the recorded music that was featured in the -- oh, I think in the lounge, you know.
Uh-huh.
He said that there should be some musicians there, working.
Uh-huh.

Of course we had a double side to it, because when the strike happened, all of the stars that later became stars, the singers, were just like side men in those days. Frank Sinatra, Dick Haymes. You know, they were just on the stand, because the band leaders ran the whole thing. And after the record industry found out that they could do without musicians, then the whole scene changed and the singers became stars. And then here comes -- oh, hi-fi, at that time. Then into stereo. So consequently you could get better music at home than you could get in a dance hall. Because the engineers found a way to make the music sound better. And excuse this -- I think I have a little nasal drip here that's slowing me up a little bit.
Then as time went along, you know -- of course you have to adjust to what you have to. As the industry changes,

you know. You know, our industry is very flexible. It goes within seasons. Now there's always a -- a real stabilizing thing is like you take the people that I knew, like the Ellingtons, the Louis Armstrongs and all those kind of people, they lasted no matter what happened. Because still the ear is the best judge of all of it, and the communication with the people, with the public, you know. We don't know when we're doing it, as I said once before. And you gave me compliments. I had no idea that the public is going to receive it that way one way or the other. You know, this whole thing is a big audition, you know.
(Laughter)
It's a big audition all the way, because you're never any better than your last performance.
It keeps it exciting, though.

Yeah, you keep driving yourself up the wall, I'll tell you that. You know, you try to find something new, and if you think you've got something new, somebody's done it a hundred years before, and you say, "Gee, I thought I was the first one to do that." I laugh at myself a lot of times.

When you were on the 20th Century Limited, you were going to Chicago with the Stuff Smith Trio, and John Levy lost his ticket, and you said this was your first trip, you and John, this was the first time you'd been to
New York City.
Yes.
Then what happened? You said there was crowd waiting to meet you at the station?
No, at the Onyx Club, that opening night.
Oh.

Oh, I have something funny to tell you about that. As soon as we got to New York and got established where we were going to stay, or live, and in those days New York was so beautiful, I knew then I was never going to go back to Chicago. Just to see my people and my father and whatever, but I wasn't about to go back to the midwest, because there was a warmness about New York, and an excitement. Your blood started circulating. That's the only way I can describe it, you know. And John and I, we just -- we had a good time going through all the clubs. We had a couple of days before we were to open, and there was Art Tatum with his trio, with Slam Stewart and Tiny Grimes, and there was Dizzy Gillespie across the street, and Erroll Garner wasn't too far away from us. And Coleman Hawkins and Don Byas, playing together, which was quite a tenor treat. And Thelonius Monk was playing piano. And we just didn't see this in Chicago, you know. We saw -- even though the clubs in New York were just made over cellars or whatever you might want to call them, but there was that atmosphere, the sophistication.
What year was this, when you got to New York?
1944. And John kids me. He tries -- he says, "You know, Jimmy, you're getting old." Now it's 35 years ago. And I just tell him, I say, "Look, no matter how old I get I will never be as old as you."
(Laughter)

That's the only answer, and that's the only thing that slows him up, you know. So I can almost remember every moment of it. Then we -- John and I used to get on the subway. We thought we were sightseeing, but how can you see anything underground? And we would go uptown in the Bronx and go way downtown and look at the Statue of Liberty, and all these things that we'd seen by postcard.
Uh-huh.

And then looking at the Empire State Building. Boy, that was like Alice in Wonderland. And the enthusiasm of youth at that time, you know? Because I used to listen to the Glenn Miller Orchestra, the Army orchestra he had before he went overseas, you know, and I liked Glenn Miller's work, and I was allowed to go into the NBC Radio Center, you know, and look at the scores and everything. You know, I was just -- they just let me in. And I was so surprised to see -- that's one thing about New York, you would see the biggest of people right next door to you. You know, you wouldn't see it in other

cities. And I'd run into guys like Paul Whiteman in the elevator, and you know, people that you just knew of. And they talked with you, you know, and said, 'Wait, look, I'm going across the street and have a beer and a corned beef sandwich. Want to join me?' And I'm sitting there looking ga-ga, you know?
(Laughter)

It's funny. Then after awhile I began to get tied into the lifestyle of that community, and when I went back to Chicago, gee whiz, it looked like a farm town, even though it's still a big, major city. But it just -- well, it was nothing like New York.
Didn't have that spirit.
No. It was nothing like New York. And I believe that New York is still the same. I haven't been back there for years.
I think it is.
Yeah, I think it's still the same. It just had to go through its financial transitions, but the culture is still there, I believe.
And the spirit of the people.
Yeah. It's a boss city, you know.
Uh-huh.
So, I want to set some time aside for myself to go back, even if it's no more than a visit. And I have a
You were mentioning Milt Hinton off the tape. How far back do you and Milt Hinton go?

Okay. Now, I think I mentioned one thing to you off the tape, was -- in Stanley Dance's book, "The World of Duke Ellington," where Milt Hinton and Ray Nance went to the same high school together, and Ray Nance was a phenomenal talent, as we both know.
Yes.

But he mentioned in that book, he says he couldn't move to the first chair because the guy that really held the first chair down was the -- became a very famous bass player, Milton Hinton. And that was a -- I don't know if Milt even knows this was stated by Nance, because I haven't talked to Milt lately.
Uh-huh.
Now, as far as going back with him, oh, boy. I've been knowing Milt since about the '40s. Because John Levy and Milt went to school together, you know.
Uh-huh.
And that's how I knew him.
So you knew him in Chicago.
Yeah. Well, no, I met him in New York. I knew of him in Chicago. Because he was one of the prominent musicians that left Chicago and became successful.
You were telling me that you and Milt called each other Judge.
Yeah.
How did that come about?

Oh, I don't know. Let's see, how did -- it's almost like a standard nickname for each other. You know, Milt has a very high voice. "Hey, Judge?" That's the way he sounds, you know. And I said, "Hey, Judge." And he sent me a birthday card, as I was telling you. He says, "I hereby sentence you to 30 days of good music." And I've got to call him back, because I didn't know that he knew when my birthday was. That was a real pleasant surprise, you know? But you'd be surprised -- well, to watch him work, as of today, I told John Levy, I said, "Man, you should see Milt A." And he looks like a teenager.
Uh-huh.
And he's playing like one. He's got that great positive attitude, and you can't beat that, really.
A lot of enthusiasm.

Yeah. He's got it. It's built in him, you know? And he's so well rounded as a musician, I don't think you're going to find many any better than Milt, or as good. Because he's -- in fact, when I was beginning to write, back east, Milt was my contractor. I used to split it with Milt, when Milt was too busy I would get Clarke Terry.
Uh-huh.

But Milt was the chief contractor, and we began to get very close, you know. I don't know whether I told this story, over at Milt's house, but with Perry Bradford and Eubie Blake. Did we tape this story?

You told me, but I can't remember whether the tape was on. I don't think so. No, I think you told me the story right when we were playing back your reference to Eubie before. No, it's not on the tape.

Oh, this is a funny story. It's a very funny story. Well, Perry Bradford -- a lot of people know who Eubie Blake is, but Perry Bradford had written -- he's written some old time songs that have become standards. And -- but he was always a hustler. He was always trying to tell Eubie where to put his money. He says, "This guy's name is Chase." He's talking about the Chase National Bank. He says -- he's talking to Eubie, this is Perry talking to Eubie. He says, "But, Cos, --" he called him Cos -- he said, "Cos, you've got to give your reference." So Eubie says, "Let that guy give me reference because this is my money." So all right, they used to hang quite a bit. And then -- this was on -- it was on a weekend, and Perry Bradford was sitting on a curb, downtown, around Times Square, and this goes way back to the days where the subway was only a nickel. And he's sitting there, he has a check in his hand, a royalty check for $18,000.00, but he

doesn't have a nickel in his pocket to get home. And he's sitting there shaking his head. He's a black man, but he turned white as a sheet, because he's got all this money and he can't move, you know. So Eubie gave him I think it was a dollar, maybe a dollar and forty-six, cents, something like that, to get to the Bronx, and this was like in 1920 and 1921, and Perry got home. Oh, he made a whole lot of money since then, but he never paid Eubie back.
And Eubie still remembers.

Yeah. He says, 'You know, this guy never paid me my money back.' Wasn't but $1.46. So now this all ties in with Milt Hinton. So Milt had -- they were coming to my house in Long Island, so Milt said, 'Well, bring him by my house.' I said okay. We all went by there and Milt's wife Mona, they were cooking and making a barbecue, and the way Eubie told it, well as you know, he's a great comedian anyway. He had everybody in stitches, just the way he just told it, you know, the way he told the story. So then Milt turned around and got Perry Bradford by his house and he told the same story the same way.
(Laughter)
And I said, 'Milt, you've got a whole lot of history here.' Oh, yeah, we had a whole lot of laughs.
You mentioned that you had your first conducting lessons from Eubie.
Oh, yeah.
How did that happen? Did you -- why did you decide to learn conducting? Was it a point in your career that you wanted to start conducting or --
Yes.
-- you needed to, or was that when you were with Sarah, or --
No, just a desire.
I see.
Just a thing that I wanted to do. I always felt in my heart that I was going to be a writer. And if you're going to be a writer you have to learn how to conduct your material.
Uh-huh.

And to interpret it. And to go to school and learn how. So consequently when I was with Sarah I just took correspondence courses at NYU, to keep myself going, you know. Because they used to kid me about going -- actually we'd get off of work at night, about going home and going to bed early. Because I had homework to do.
Uh-huh.

And later on, when I did some albums with Sarah, then she found out. I told her -- we call her Sass, that's her nickname, you know. I said, 'Sass, I just had to study because I had to advance plans.' Just couldn't stay in one I

spot, you know, even though I loved the way she sang. But I couldn't -- I couldn't stay in that one spot. As I'm restless now. I can't stay in one spot now. I don't know where I'm going, but I want to go somewhere.
But you're doing a variety of things, aren't you?

Oh, yes. But that was like a major step in a particular direction. It wasn't too much variety there. It was just a -- maybe a switch over to another echelon of the industry, just to walk away from the piano and get up in front of the orchestra.
Uh-huh.

You know? And there were times I'd write some music that was too hard for me to play and I'd get Hank Jones to play it. I'd say, 'Gee, Hank can play this better than I can.' I can write it, but sometimes I'd look at it and I'd say, 'Gee, whiz, did I write this?'
(Laughter)
Somebody said, 'Well, you wrote it. You should be able to play it.' I said, 'No, go get Hank Jones. He's a real professional pianist.' They say piano player, but he's a pianist.
In fact I used to surround Milt and Hank with oh, maybe 15 or 20 strings, and maybe sometimes five and eight brass, large orchestras. And they were the anchor men, and I

would have an anchor man in each section, and they were all first class musicians. And I think that we underrate the American musician, because when it comes to instant music, instant perfection, I don't know where you can get it as fast as you can get it in the States. These guys can play jazz, they can improvise, they can sight read, they can do it all. They really spoiled me as a writer, because out here -- when I say out here I mean in Los Angeles, the same thing. Back in New York, the same thing. And it's really great to -- after you what I call sweat over a score or work over a score all night and all day, and go in and just drop your hand down, on the first downbeat, and to hear it come back at you, and you know you're going to get paid. That's not the problem. But the payment is to hear it. You know, it's a personal satisfaction, and there's always a little edge that it may not come off, so you have to have a recourse, one way or the other, you know.
The projects, when you would put together a large orchestra like that that you would build around Milt and Hank, what were the projects?

Oh, albums with Joe, Sarah -- Joe Williams, Sarah Vaughan, and Mel Torme. Oh, gee whiz, I can't -- I can't remember all the acts I've written for. But I have so much gratitude towards the musicians that performed it. And it's more than just the music and the normal friendship,

but it's the professional attitude in the studio. There was a statement in this last album with Kenny Burrell (BONEHEAD). She said it in such a way, I wasn't paying any attention to what he said until I read it again. He says, "Jimmy Jones, Musical Director, handled it very gently."
Uh-huh.

But firm, to keep the discipline, to keep the whole thing in order. That's the way I've been used to doing it, just be firm. Now and then you'll get somebody that gets a little out of step, and you call a five minute break or something and pull one individual aside, so your deportment doesn't get away from you, and keep some decorum in the studio.
Uh-huh.
You know.
Well, that's an art.
It's --
Handling, coordinating.
Yes.
Directing music with a large number of people, and sometimes you've got personalities and temperaments to deal with. You shouldn't have to, but sometimes you do.
Yes.
When you work with artists.
Yes. And the main thing is not to -- to

never let it go downhill within your recording time, you know? Just don't let it rub off on the other musicians, because you'll get a -- not a negative performance, but a lesser performance than you normally would get, you know? Because musicians are sensitive. They know what's going on. You know, they're quite aware. But to keep it kind of --

Uh-huh.
And I said, gee whiz, they must be a hundred years old or something, you know?

No -- well, okay. But it was just nice to know, and they tell me that the house is still standing there and people are still living in it, you know?

This was before Lunceford went to Fisk University. And my father was teaching at Le Moine College in Memphis at that point, you know. It was all in Tennessee. No, I don't think so. I don't think my father realized that he was going to become what he became at that point.
Uh-huh.
He was quite young, you know.
Uh-huh.
And consequently they just -- well, after we moved to Chicago there was no way to stay in touch, you know. Geographically we were in two different places, you know.
Yeah. Have you happened to remember

I think her name was Miss Barrett, if I can remember, -- I have to remember her because she was tough.

Yes.

Oh, we had -- there were about 50 to 75 pieces. And I was the bass player, one of the bass players. We had like four bass players, you know.
Uh-huh.
And we used to play operettas and things, you know. I thought I wanted to be a bass player, but in those times it cost too much money, so --
You mean to buy a bass?
Yeah. So the piano was still in the house, so I had to go back to piano, you know?
How do you feel now? Do you wish you had studied bass or kept with the bass or --
No, I like piano better.
You certainly seem to have a magnificent affinity for the piano.
Yeah, I like piano, because it's -- the knowledge you get from it. Bass, you only play one note at a time. And piano you play ten.
(Laughter)

Ten notes. You've got two hands there, you know. So consequently it's almost like orchestrating, you know. Of course in later years, since I've been writing, I don't write near the piano. That was very interesting, when you mentioned that before. Did you -- I can't remember -- did you mention who the teachers were that weaned you from the piano?
Well, one was Marion Evans who was a great string writer and quite a friend.
I think you did mention him.
And then Rudolph Schramm at NYU. He was a Schillinger teacher, you know.
Yes. You mentioned him. You mentioned being on the road with Sarah and Basie with the Birdland show. Do you remember what year that was?
Oh, it was about in the middle '50s, I think. Because after I -- I went back with Sarah, after I'd been in the hospital.

Oh, let's see, we did the big show in '51. A lot of people could remember that. That was with Ellington, Nat Cole, Sarah, the Marie Bryant Dancers. It was the first big package show. And then I became sick with tuberculosis, so that took a couple of years out, and I went back with Sarah. Sarah just held the job for me, no matter who played. She wanted me back, you know.
Uh-huh.

And we got a trio, and the Birdland tours started coming around, with -- that's the band that Basie had with Thad Jones and Frank Foster, Frank Wess, Ernie Wilkins. And Joe Williams was the singer. Quite a package.
Yes.
A very strong package, you know.
You mentioned Ella getting standing ovations in Hamburg. Do you remember what year that was, because it helps to sort of put these things in perspective if we can remember the years.
All right, I joined Ella -- oh, boy, let me -- this is '78, right?
Uh-huh.

In sixty -- about '65 -- '64 or '65, somewhere right around there. A little earlier. No, no, a little earlier. In -- I think that's when I first went to Europe with her, when she was getting those standing ovations.
Uh-huh. Okay. Now.

Like I had gotten to the point where I began to know London and Paris so well, I knew how to get on the Metro, you know the subway --
Uh-huh.
-- and go where I wanted to go. And the
subway in London.

Oh.

And we'd just pick up whomever the band had. At that point, I think they had Illinois Jacquet's band, and I think it was Joe Jones, who was the famous drummer with Basie, and I think Al Lucas was the bass player. So we were never in trouble.
No.
(Laughter)
We always had good music with us, you know.

Oh, like in -- let's see, I guess he had five saxophones and six brass.

Yes.

Uh-huh.
And I think he stayed in that club for about 12 years.
Yeah.

And it was nationwide, the exposure was nationwide, you know. Uh-huh.

Uh-huh.
You know, there seems to be a pattern. We don't know why.

Kentucky State.
Kentucky State. Excuse me. Pardon me. Kentucky State.
Yeah.
But who else -- I guess that was when, what -- was that when you first became familiar with Cab's band, was the radio broadcasts, or --
Oh, I'd heard it --

Yeah, well there were some guys that preceeded me on piano, you know.
Uh-huh.
But it was Ellington orientated, you know.
Uh-huh.
