One date, then we had dinner, then we came back and did the second one, and when we came back, Duke had told Bobby Boyd, the road manager, you know, to go get Dizzy Gillespie, because he wanted some discipline. And he got it. When Dizzy walked in the studio, everybody was sitting up like tin soldiers, you know? But now Clarke Terry didn't have to worry about it, you know, because Clarke could handle himself. And that was one of the best trumpet sections that Duke had. He had Clarke Terry, Shorty Baker, Ray Nance and Cat Anderson.
That's a hell of a section.

Yeah. But they weren't there on the first part of the date, you know. So Duke just said, well, he wanted to be sure he had another trombone player, -- or, a trumpet player, so he called Dizzy in. But by that time he had five trumpets, you know?
Uh-huh.

But everybody had to play and pay attention. Like there was another time when Duke said -- he had two bass players. He had Junior Ragland and Al Lucas, but Junior Ragland would get drunk, so Duke said, 'I'd better hire another bass player so I can be sure I have one.'
(Laughter)
So Al and Ragland started going out and
getting drunk together.
(Laughter)
Duke said, 'Gee, I'm paying two bass players and neither one of them are here.'
(Laughter)
Oh, boy, that was a very comical scene, you know, in a lot of ways. But musically, that was my favorite orchestra.
You said -- you're quoted in the inaudible book as saying that when you were writing for Harry Belafonte, that you approached your writing there as Duke did, for sound effects rather than the notes.
Yes. Yes.
Or something to that effect.
Yes.
Do you want to expand on that?

Well, I'll tell you. With Harry I had to make a 180 degree turn, because he had been like Calypso, and then writing for television, and the idea was to overwrite, because it's easier to take out than to have to write it in the studio.
Uh-huh.
You know, you can always -- see, one of the basic things I think in writing, if you look at your manuscript, you always have -- well, all you need is two or

three elements and you have to keep them going. They can just be expanded and be larger. You have your rhythm section working, you have your soloists working, and that's two elements right there. And then you have the orchestra working. Now, if it gets too busy it sounds like scrambled eggs, you know?
Uh-huh.
So if the -- the main thing was to keep it transparent.
Uh-huh.

Like I used to study Rimsky-Korsakoff's book on orchestrating, and I think he was one of the greatest in keeping it transparent, where you can understand it all, you know? And to learn, don't be afraid of simplicity, you know?
Uh-huh.

Because, well, when you go through the early age you think you want to prove something, and oh, there are some things I've written before, years ago, that I won't even play, you know, because as you go along you get the experience on playbacks and hearing them back. Well, with Harry I learned that, and Duke used to always say -- he'd tell some writers -- he never did bother me at all. I think he liked the way I wrote. He'd say, 'Too many notes,' you know?
Uh-huh.
And he was right. You know, as you go

along and become seasoned, you begin to realize just write only what's logical. Like in having a conversation, if you write only what's logical, you just go -- well, you have to communicate with the ear, the ear of the public, or the people that are not participating in our field, so make it so they understand it, and pretty soon you'll enjoy it more yourself.
You said Duke always thought in terms of sound effects, or total sound, and didn't think in notes.

Yeah, I think he was an effect man, and that's what attracted me to them quite a bit, because everybody else, when I was coming up, thought in terms of notes, but Duke had effects. There was one time he had a funny line. He'd -- you know, horns have different ranges, and the bass trombone player, Chuck Connors, Duke had written a part for him and he kept going down, down, down, to the bottom register of his horn, and Chuck says, "Duke these other notes that you've got here are down below and they're off the horn." And Duke says, "It can't be, because there's a note down there. Let them make a new trombone." "The tuba plays it."
(Laughter)
So he was right, though, you know? There are notes down there you know?
Uh-huh.
And I read a book, Dr. Toch (PHONETIC). I used to study his book quite often, and he had some examples
(Ernst Toch)

where Richard Wagner used to do that. You know, he would write a viola part or a violin part, to go, keep going down, and the guy, you know, just runs right off the register. Because if you go down just to the bottom there's a tendency to psychologically stop, you know, but he just wanted him to go and play off the horn, really loud -- off the violin, really loud. And it's a psychological thing, just read it straight on through, you know? And I learned that. I learned a lot of things from studying like that and a lot of things from Ellington, a lot of things from Lenny Hayton, when I was with Lena.
Do you think Duke did things like that psychologically, writing the music in a way that would affect the players?
Yes.
Like what, could you give me an example?
Well, I was -- let me see. I'm going to go back -- this was a collective situation, on the Basie and Duke.
Did you write some of that stuff?

No, I didn't. I didn't know they were recording that day. I think Bud Johnson called me up and told me to come over to Columbia Record studios. But I think when Duke wrote those clashes, when I said that Marshall Royal said he was splitting atoms?
Uh-huh.

He did that on purpose, because Basie plays kind of pure, you know. There's a difference -- but they sound good playing it. It's just that the -- Ellington just wrote that way. And okay, now there was -- of course there's going to be some competitive feeling, even though Duke and Basie were tight. But the pride that the guy has in his craft.
Uh-huh.

Two of the best bands. So Duke would write those high tension chords, and I think that's one of the reasons why he would -- like I was saying, Thad Jones would play, and his reed section would play behind Thad.
Uh-huh.
He would never let it get to a contest. That's the reason it came out that way, you know?
Well, he would never play a so-called battle of the bands.
No, no.
He believed that in art there should not be comparison.

No, no. I agree with him totally on that. Because after all, in the final analysis I think that all of these guys are first class, you know, and after you get up in a certain area, it's a matter of choice, you know, a
matter of who you like the best, you know?
Uh-huh.

And that's philosophical after that, you know, it's not factual necessarily, you know? Like the great Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra was quite an organization, you know? And in my early days I used to argue about Ellington and tell the guys that Duke was the greatest, Duke was the greatest this, that and the other, but then other guys would argue right with me that Lunceford was the greatest. And I hear some of the new things that Capitol and Time-Life put out on Lunceford, and they've got the guys around here right now that can play and write just like they did in those days, and they sound good. Still. Time is a great thing, you know?
Uh-huh.

If it can hold up with time, you know? So -- but getting back to the question you asked me, as far as Duke doing these things with the men, he was very perceptive. If he could see a bad mood coming, he knew how to agitate.
Uh-huh.

He really knew how to agitate. Well, you know, it was some years back -- I hope this doesn't offend anybody -- but Stan Kenton -- the times I've been around Stan Kenton, he's been very nice to me, you know, a nice guy. But he made a statement. I think he just -- he didn't really mean it as what people made out of it, you know. He says, 'There's
a new minority --," this was after the jazz poll.
In Downbeat.
Yeah, I guess it was Downbeat. But then they took it to the New York Post, you know?
Uh-huh.
And so Duke and Stan Kenton were --
Wait a minute. The whole quote was there's a new minority and what's the rest of it?
The new minority was the white race he said, the white players.
What, jazz musicians?

Yeah. So there was a battle of jazz booked in Detroit, at the Graystone Ballroom, I think. And Duke got in front of the bus to agitate his players. He says, "We're not having a battle of jazz tonight. We're going to a race riot."
(Laughter)
You know? And he fired the guys up.
Uh-huh.
You know? He really fired them up. I says, "Oh, man, he's --," but I don't think Kenton meant that, not that way, you know.
Uh-huh.
Because I've spent some time with Kenton since I've been out here, you know.
What have you done for him?
Well, it's just with the neophonic thing, you know, with Wes, and his inviting me to some of his sessions and things, you know, and he became ill for awhile, you know. But --
Back to Duke's writing. It was only partially kept in order, the library. I mean Joe Benjamin (PHONETIC) was trying to put it together --
Yeah.
-- so it could be found and referred to.
Yeah.
But he got called out on the road to work with the band before he finished his project of trying to get everything together at least in terms of music.
Yeah.
So the condition of what Duke wrote and the band book, I understood from Tom Whaley (PHONETIC), nobody -- there's nobody around who knows how it's supposed to get together.
Yes.
And there's only a few people who could -- Tom of course is blind. He can't tell anymore.
No.
(Inaudible). There's you and there's
Herbie Jones and there's John Sanders, and isn't that just about the extent of people who would understand the music that Duke left?
Yes, I think so.
Herbie Jones used to arrange and copy.
Yeah, that's right. Herbie worked close with the old man.
And --
John Sanders.
Who is a priest full time.
Yeah.

But isn't that -- is there anybody else who would know? Understand what went with what and what belonged in some of the missing places and how it all fits together? I think (unaudible) was the one that told me that Duke used to write in kind of hieroglyphics. If you don't know what he means, he says, the average person, no matter how fine a musician he is, could walk up to an Ellington score and not know what it means.

Yes, that's right. That's very true, because there was one time I was doing some things with Johnny Hodges, you know, with a small group, about eight or ten pieces, and Tom Whaley -- Duke was living next door to me, and Tom Whaley was living about, oh, maybe three blocks away, and Billy Strayhorn. We were all living in one area. So I had to

take these scores over to Tom's to get them copied, and Tom says, "Take a look at this. This is one of Duke's scores." And I looked at it, and I said, "Tom, this can't work." He said, "You've been listening to it for the last 25 years."
(Laughter)
But you can't hear it when it's played, you know? I looked at it on paper and I said, "This thing is supposed to work, man."
(Laughter)
He says, "It's what I'm here for." I said, "But it doesn't sound like that when they play it." He said, "No, but that's what's there."
(Laughter)

And Strayhorn told me that Duke taught him extremes. Like he would put Carney's (PHONETIC) -- the baritone, normally everybody puts the baritone on the bottom, but he would put Paul on the bottom and put Carney up in the middle of the section and get a completely different sound. Put him in, you know, different, odd registers. You know? And those guys had great sounds. Oh, they had -- they all had great tones, you know? And I may have said this before -- I think I did say it before -- I had written this thing for -- it was really for Ella and just for Duke, on the -- "Ella At Duke's Place." And Ella liked the arrangement very much, but she didn't realize I was voicing like the old man, you know?

And she took the arrangement to some other orchestra and I heard it and I said, "Ella take that out of the book, because it doesn't sound good. It sounds like, you know, it sounds very like what we call vanilla." Just nothing, you know. Because if you don't have a Harry Carney or a Johnny Hodges Gonzalves in there and Paul Gonzales and all that, it doesn't mean anything. The personalities are not there. And --
Well, Duke definitely wrote for the sound of the individual.
Yeah. And I did the same way. But that's the objection I have to studio writing, even though that's instant music, sight reading and everything.
Uh-huh.

But you don't get those personalities in there. You know, you don't get the personalities, and it makes it harder on the arranger, because you have to put your own thing into it to make it a little fresh or different, you know?
Uh-huh.
You have to do it from the manuscript.
Uh-huh.
Because normally if you do it like with Ellington's thing, well he did it with the manuscript but he had the players to do it too. You know, that made quite a difference.
Like when somebody had to go, leave the band, like that arrangement would play.
Yeah, that's right.
(Inaudible)
It was written for a new voice.
Yeah, that's right. Because that was conceived for this one particular person, you know?
Tyree said he was on the band 3 months.
Uh-huh. (Inaudible). -- and he'd see Duke listening to him.
Uh-huh. Yeah.
And I guess finding out what Tyree's ideas were like and his range and what his sound was and so on (Inaudible).
Yeah.
(Inaudible)

Yeah. Well, Bill Berry has a funny story. When he came in the band. Well, he wasn't used to these personalities, you know, so there were no trumpet parts for him and those that he saw had cigarette burnings all over them, you know, and Cat and the guys, they wouldn't say anything to him, so he said he was really confused. Said, "This is the greatest band in the world, but I don't understand it," you know? So he would -- he'd just sit there and Duke would -- told him, he says, "Put your horn to your mouth. Dress my bandstand up, whether you've got anything to play or not." And then later on Duke kept telling him -- he'd say, "What should I play on this?" He says, "Find a note." Then he was
testing his ear.
Uh-huh.
You know, that's what he was really doing. "Find a note. See what you can squeeze in there." Then he could find out what latitude he had to work with, you know?
Uh-huh.
And eventually he got -- he got some stuff around Bill.
Yes.
You know, he found him.

And Bill told me on his first night with the band, he didn't know, not having a book, didn't know what to play and asked Cat what he should put on the end of the number, and Cat said, "Pick a note that sounds wrong and play it."

Yeah. Yeah. Well, that -- that was -- that's what the band -- it kept developing and developing into what it became, and I'm going back to when I first started listening. "Black Beauty," that was in the last '20s. Around Chicago we used to listen to Ellington all the time, you know?
Uh-huh.
And we could see it coming. Of course the band was much smaller at that point, but they still had as much -- that basic excitement was there.
Uh-huh.
It was there all the time, and I still have to say that a lot of it was due to the leader.
Uh-huh.

You know. To the leader. He knew who he wanted and what he wanted. I don't know whether Harry Carney ever told you this or not, that -- how Duke conned Carney's parents in Boston to get him on the road.
I know that he (Inaudible), but I don't know exactly what he said.

Well, I spent time with Carney at his home in Boston, and he used to tell me how Duke had -- because he was young, you know? And when Carney got out on the road with the band, that was his life and that was it, you know? And he developed, oh, boy, he developed into a monster on the baritone. Oh, there's a picture of him when he was in Boston, he was a kid. You could tell it was Carney because he had definite certain features about him. About five or six pieces. And it's in Eubie Blake's front room. Yeah, Eubie knew the guy who was the band leader then, you know?
Uh-huh.
But I said -- right there in Brooklyn. And I told Eubie, I said, 'That's Harry Carney there.' He said, 'Is that right? I never met Harry Carney.'
I'll be darned.
And I said, 'That's Duke's baritone player.' And Carney looked like he should have on knickers
or something. (Laughter) That's how young he looked, you know? (Laughter)
And Eubie -- oh, incidentally, today he's 95.
I know. It was on television this morning.
Yeah. Well, Teddy Edwards called me up and he's still in good shape.
That was a shame, they cut him off right in the middle of the interview when the time was up (Inaudible).
Yeah.
But it was good to see him, and he was sparkling like he does.

Well, I think he did a -- he was on A.M. the other morning, they had a birthday cake for him, and I imagine Johnny Carson might say something about him, because when he became 90 and he wasn't even here, Carson spoke of it, you know.
Uh-huh.
Oh, Eubie, he's a very popular man.
Well, he's charming.
Yeah, he is. Great personality. So I'm going to call him, you know.
Do you know what Duke said to Carney's parents?
I don't know. Carney just told me the story. He says that Duke was such a charmer, you know --
Uh-huh.
And evidently Carney, he was close knit with his parents, you know, it was a close family.
Uh-huh.
And then maybe that's the reason Duke took up the slack as the father.
There really was a father-son kind of relationship, I think all the way to the end.
Yeah.
I mean Harry used to wait for Duke to tell him what to do.
Yeah.
(Inaudible) -- I don't know, his father figure, his --
Yeah, his father -- the image.
Yeah. I think he was -- I don't know how close he was to his real father, but he really -- I think Duke became sort of his father.
Yeah.
And he was, you know, up in his 50s and 60s, he was still looking to Duke for the answers.

Well, you know, that can happen. Because I just adopted Duke as a father when I was a kid, and my father got crazy about the music so much he would always keep me posted where Duke was playing, or you know, when I was away in school, and what he did, he would send me the clippings and the publicity.
I saw a reference to that in (inaudible) book.
Yeah. And so my parents, you know, they just said, 'Well, James has got somebody to look up to,' in case anything would happen to them, you know?
Uh-huh.

And I would have something to lean on. And it worked. It worked out that way. Only up to the point where Duke wanted me to go on the road. And I told him, I said, 'Edward it's too late now. I think if we had both started this when I was much, much younger, and something to build on.' You know.
Uh-huh.
It would have been at a better time in both of our lives to make it. But he still -- he still liked my work. He still called on me for -- you know?
Uh-huh.
So -- in fact, I have some musicians tell me, 'You know, you're an expert on Duke.' I say, 'No such thing
as that." You know. We had some books open here, and one of "The Esquire Jazz Book," and it has an introduction them is (Inaudible) of that famous photograph in Harlem of all the jazzmen.
Yes. Yes.
You told me you were going to tell me about that day.
Oh, yes. Well, I don't know what other pictures they have in there. In the original Esquire book they had a whole two pages to Charlie Parker, and I don't know whether they have it here or not.
No, they don't have it on here. I have that, the original, but we were looking at this --
And then they had another page or so to Duke, you know?
Uh-huh.

Well, I just got this call, you know how New York is, you get a phone call you don't know what it is or how important it's going to be. There's no big production about anything, you know. So I got a -- I think Nat Hentoff called me and told me where to be. I was there and I saw all of these musicians, you know, getting together. Had no idea what it was about. And I think Milt Hinton, the great bass player, took movies of everybody moving about, color movies.
I think you said Milt showed them to you.

Oh, yes, they were great, you know? And I think Sonny Greer was moving around, talking. You could see him clowning. Because they're sounds. You know he had sound tracks on them. And let me see, what else can I think about that day.
Well, how long did it take to get the picture together, to get everybody lined up and up the steps of the --
Reasonably fast. It was surprising. Because anytime you can get all these drunks together --
(Laughter)
And everybody in there is -- we had -- you know how the pattern is. But they got them together.
What happened afterward? Did anybody get together musically?
No. We just went on back home and went on about our ways, you know?
You've got the makings of some great music there.

Oh, yes. Very prominent people. Very great talents. In fact I have at home some pictures of -- I don't know who took these. They were taken on the stairs. I think I was talking to Horace Silver and Basie and Jo Jones and Hank Jones and I were talking together, you know?
Uh-huh.
I have them at home. And -- somebody else was taking pictures that day, you know? But they must have known that this was going to come off. I didn't know until the last minute, you know?
Uh-huh. There's another picture in Dan Morgenstern's book.
Oh, yes.
Of you and Johnny Hodges in a recording studio. Is that the date that you mentioned where you conducted and Duke wasn't there and --
Yeah.
Is that the studio in New Jersey you said?
No, this was the one in New York. We did two albums.
Oh, I thought that looked like New York.
Yeah. This studio is on 42nd Street and I was -- what am I doing -- I'm straightening out some notes at the podium, you know?
Uh-huh.
I called this date, the first date, at 9:00 o'clock in the morning, because -- on a Monday, because psychologically if the guys have been off on the weekend they might be hanging over a little bit.
Uh-huh.

Because I had -- let's see, who did I have on there? I had Snooky, Snooky Young, Ernie Royal, Bill Berry, Tony Studd, Frank Wess, Jerome Richardson, Jimmy Hamilton. Who else? Oh, Milt Hinton, Hank Jones. It was a good band. And Johnny Hodges playing first on it, you know. So I came in with the -- you know how you go in shops and buy little trinket things, where they have little quotations on there, and I just came and hung it on the -- I had it hanging on this thing, I think. I'm not sure. Well, where everybody could see it. What it said on there, now everybody's married, "For every great man in the world there's a woman telling him he's wrong."
(Laughter)
I don't care what he does. And that broke up everybody. It got them started, got them in a jovial mood, you know? And we got a -- we came up with a good date.
It's too bad that isn't legible in the picture. That's funny.

Yeah. So, well, we started at 9:00 o'clock, see, because usually in New York -- I don't know how it is now -- dates would go like 10:00 to -- three hours unless it goes overtime -- 10:00 to 1:00, then 2:00 to 5:00, and then there's a dinner break. You know, everybody --
Uh-huh.

And then it starts from 7:00 to 10:00 at night. Now, you have to watch that 7:00 to 10:00 at night, because they go to Jim and Andy's and go to the bar. You have to catch them early in the morning, get them early in the day.
Uh-huh.
To get the mileage out of them, you know?
Uh-huh.

Because I remember there was one time when I think it was Grady Tate and Ernie Roth, had an early morning date, then there was a whole lot of time in between, until 7:00 o'clock at night, and they got into Jim and Andy's and started eating and getting logey and drinking and partying, till they had to send somebody in their place, because they couldn't cut that date in that shape.
(Laughter)
And there was no way for them to do it, you know? See, you have to be -- it's dangerous, you know. You got to know how to do that, especially in Manhattan.
Yeah.
Like Milt and some of the more experienced guys, Milt Hinton, they would always eat.
Uh-huh.
Eat. And Milt's wife, Mona, would keep some -- he was eating vitamin pills like peanuts, you know?
Uh-huh.

To keep his energy up, keep him in good shape, you know? And so consequently they never got in any trouble. They would have their drinks and have their fun, but they never got into any trouble by being run down or anything, you know?
Uh-huh.

Johnny Hodges used to come by my house and he would sit by my piano, and we were getting tunes together, it was a date, you know, and he used to play so very heavy. He had a big sound. But he could play so soft that you couldn't hear him at times. He sat right in our apartment, and we had a corduroy case, and you'd sit next to the apartment, and you couldn't even -- say if you were sitting from here, as far as that piano is there, and that's about six feet, you could hardly hear him.
Gee.
Yeah, he could play real soft, you know. And my wife used to get nervous when he'd come around, even though she knew him. She'd known him back in the show days. But she admired him so much.
Uh-huh.

You know, there was just sheer admiration. And Johnny would sit there and we'd play and work things out. But we had a -- we had a very good relationship. And there was one -- one album that I made, it was Johnny Hodges
Billy Strayhorn and the Orchestra. Now that was done in New Jersey. Where I played piano, you know?
Uh-huh.
And --
Did Billy play too?
No, he didn't play. I played the whole thing. And -- well, we had like -- we had three, like a trio of piano players in the organization by then, you know?
Uh-huh.
But Duke was working at Basin Street East, and Duke was getting upset a little bit about it, because all the guys would go over to Johnny's and be on time for his record dates.
(Laughter)
And Duke said, "Well, why is everybody playing for my saxophone player and on time for his dates and late on mine?" And somebody said, "Well, Johnny pays off quicker than you do."
(Laughter)
Which was true. Johnny Hodges had his business together. It was completely in order, you know?
Uh-huh.
And --
Yeah, Duke had that problem of not making the payroll on time.
Yeah.
Often.
Yeah. And then they would go out to Nut City. But you know I never had any problem with him on that?
He was never slow with your money?
Uh-huh.
He was with mine. He was with the bands. Procope quit one day in New York because he hadn't been paid in three weeks, and so --
In what, three weeks?
Uh-huh.
Gee.

That was in 1968. And so he walked out. He said he wasn't going to make the date. So Duke sent Harry Carney after him. Duke didn't go after him. Duke sent Harry Carney after him. "Bring Russell on up to the date. Have him drive with us." And so Harry had the responsibility of talking Russell back into the band.
Oh, boy.
And he did it.
(Laughter)
That was one organization, one of a kind. I don't think -- well, I don't think I'll see it anymore.
Uh-huh.
There may be one that comes along, but
No, it can't ever happen again, and that was a combination of absolutely one time people.
Yeah.
You have made a note here, Benny Goodman. What did you want to --
Oh, yes, I played with -- I did some work with Benny Goodman.
When was that?

Let me see, when -- I played in his sextet. I was with Sarah at the time, and we were -- we were in New York and we had some time off. Richard Davis played bass. They liked our trio, you know, and little Roy -- Roy Burns, I think, a little red headed drummer.
Uh-huh.
He played drums. And oh, Benny was using a trumpet with him. I can't think of his name now. Billy Butterfield.
Oh.

Yeah. And you know the way that thing worked, it was quite strange in that Teddy Wilson, as far as pianos are concerned, there's no way to -- in a sextet and a trio -- there's no way that Benny could tell a story without Teddy Wilson being in it, you know?
Uh-huh.
Then it came from Teddy Wilson to Mel Powell and -- for the sextette work, because Jess Stacy played with the big band, you know?
Uh-huh.
And then Hank Jones, and I was right behind Hank. Then I could always tell when Benny was going to call me, because Hank would call me up first. He says, "Watch it, Benny's coming."
(Laughter)
By that time Hank had refused it, you know?
(Laughter)
He'd say, "Watch it, Jimmy, here comes Benny." And -- but he was okay. It was a nice experience, nice reference, you know.
How long did you work with him?
Just during the few weeks that I was off and Sarah was off, that's all, you know. But I was supposed to go with him immediately after I got to New York with Stuff Smith.
Oh. What happened?

I wanted to stay there and get my card and get my own little reputation. And we were going back to Chicago, you know, and Teddy Wilson was -- I think he was going to teach at Julliard at that point, you know, and he recommended

Let's see, what did I do on the Bill Cosby special? Oh, yes. That goes back awhile. That was a group of singers. This was vocal writing. And I forget the name of the group now. They were on capital records and they did some work on the Cosby show, you know. I tell you what was so ironic about that. Cosby wanted one particular thing. Cosby wanted the Negro national anthem, "Lift Every Voice and Sing," you know?
Uh-huh.
And these youngsters never heard of it.
(Laughter)
And that was funny, you know? And I said,
"Gee, when I was young I couldn't walk into the house and speak to my father unless I could sing it," you know?
Uh-huh.

In my day. But these kids don't know anything about that, you know. But I taught it to them, you know. And they could sing. It was a beautiful group, and they did a good job on it. That's about the extent on that, I think.
And the Dinah Shore Peace Corps Special, what did you do on that?
Oh, this was with Harry.
Harry Belafonte.
Belafonte. Now that's going back, oh -- Peace Corps thing. Sergeant Shriver was on it. I just had to write some scores, that's all.
And the Perry Como Show?
With Ella Fitzgerald. Same thing.
Uh-huh. And under motion pictures I have, "Shaft's Big Score," which we talked about. Are there any other films that you worked on that haven't made this list yet?
Let's see. Let's see. No. Gordon Parks called me. He wanted me to join him with Tom MacIntosh on that film.
Uh-huh.
I'm trying to think, I didn't do -- didn't do any things in the studios, I mean the movie studios,

but I'm trying to remember if I'd done some television movies. Writing New York 19, and underscoring as we call it, a lot of people, talking, making love, or something, that's -- that is the same thing.
Yeah, I know.

You know. Oh, I've got a little funny story to tell you. We had -- on, "Shaft's Second Score," so they had a -- I had to write several cues in that, you know, a whole lot. So the trumpet section had swivel chairs, you know?
Uh-huh.

And they had a big, large screen. So I had written one cue for O.C. Smith, another one for Freddie Hubbard, another one for Marshall Royal, and somebody else, I forgot. So I just had chord symbols for Freddie Hubbard, you know?
Uh-huh.

And this was a funny scene where Shaft was in the bedroom with his lady. And I told him, I says -- he asked me, he said, "Jimmy, what do you want me to play on this?" I said, "Turn your chair around and look at the big screen and see what Shaft is doing and play that."
(Laughter)
He's making love in the bedroom. I said, "Play that." And he did it, you know?
Uh-huh.
Because he was facing me. And I said -- and the screen was behind them, you know?
Uh-huh.
I said, 'Just turn the chair around and play what you see.'
Uh-huh. Under conducting credits, as musical director, the first listing I see here is Kalamazoo Symphony Orchestra, Erroll Garner, guest soloist.
Yeah, that's right.
Have you worked with the symphony many times? That's the only listing I think I see here.
No.
Is that the only one or have there been others? You have Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan. Did they do any work with symphonies while you were their musical conductors?
No. They played -- I had to write a lot of symphonic scores for them.
Oh.
And they used them, you know.
Tell me about -- was this the only time you worked with Erroll, beside maybe -- well, I'm sure you knew him on 52nd Street.
Yeah.
Is this the only time you --
Yeah, this is the only time.
And was this -- how long ago was it, the Kalamazoo Symphony?
That must have been -- oh, a little after, "My People."
Yeah, around there.
Was this his first performance with symphony? I don't really remember.
You mean Erroll's?
Yeah.

What they -- I think what they had, going at that time, you know how they have those tours, Nelson Riddle, Erroll Garner -- who else was it? A couple of other big names. Were touring in the midwest with these symphony orchestras, you know?
Uh-huh.
And Erroll just wanted me to do the one in Kalamazoo with him.
Uh-huh.
And I don't think he did any more.
I don't remember hearing about Erroll and an association with symphony appearances much.
No. One of the reasons I think he wanted me to do it, because he had had problems in his style. The
way he played, conductors would listen to his right hand, which would lag, but his left hand kept the tempo.
Uh-huh.
And I knew it.
Uh-huh.
And he knew I knew it.
Uh-huh.
So he wanted to play it safe, because he's told me that a lot of the guys just lag all the time, you know, they make the orchestra lag and lose the tempo.
Uh-huh.

And you have to just conduct ahead of the orchestra to keep them even with Erroll. You know, because they'll fall behind, especially string players, because they lag and trumpet players lag back too, so you have to -- if you're going at a tempo, like, say, one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, you have to do the one, two, three, four, like, one, two, three, four, ahead, you know?
Uh-huh.
Now, with a jazz orchestra you don't have to do that, because see they hit right on the nose when you bring your hand down, you know?
Uh-huh.
But it's different with the -- oh, the first time I did some conducting for strings was with Joe
Williams. We had Ben Webster, Harry Edison on the date, you know, just to put the jazz sound in it, you know.
Uh-huh.

And I'd never conducted for them before. And I said, "Gee whiz, I wonder --," this was Roulette Records and it was a gangster company, and I said, "Boy, this better come off, or else I'll have a cement overcoat in the Hudson River.
(Laughter)
And I brought my hand down and it looks like they didn't come in till next year, because the sound doesn't come to you right away like a horn.
Uh-huh.

You know, it kind of moves around the room a little bit or something, you know. And I got -- after that I got used to it. Now it's just like eating duck soup. Because the last thing I did with Milt Jackson was a string date, you know. It came off very good. And we had Hubert Laws, Jerome Richardson, Ray Brown, Tommy Flanagan, you know. I always keep a few of the jazz tribe in there. You know. That's from whence I came.
How long did you know Erroll Garner?
Since about 1944, when I first went to New York.
Uh-huh.

That's when I first met him. He was working on 52nd Street, too. He was working towards the end of the block, and there was so much excitement. There was Erroll Garner on one end of the block and Art Tatum on the other end. And gee whiz, I didn't know which way to turn my head. I was like looking at a tennis match.
(Laughter)

So John Levy and I laugh about that today. Our first day in New York. We could only -- we only stayed up till about 12:00 o'clock, because we were so high, we were going from one bar to the other, and got so excited and looking at Art and Dizzy and all these guys at clubs, back to back, you know?
Uh-huh.

That's the way the street was laid out. And to see everybody within one block. And we just -- you know, in Chicago or something like Los Angeles, it's kind of spread out. But we -- and then to be able to talk with them, and hang out with them, on intermissions and everything, you know? So --
How about Linton Garner, was he there then?
I don't think so. But I've got to -- Linton worked with Timmy Rogers, and I didn't get a chance to really know Linton that well until the Big Show of 1951, that

first big package show. Remember the one that had Duke's band and the Marie Bryant dancers. King Cole was the headliner, Nat King Cole. I was with Sarah Vaughan. And we had -- Duke was the emcee, and we had Patterson and Jackson, comedians, Timmy Rogers, and then Stump and Stumpy, some more comedians, you know, and a dancer named Peg Leg Bates.
Uh-huh.
So it was quite a show.
I remember, yeah.
Yeah, it was quite a show.
Linton Garner and Billy Strayhorn were friends from back in Pittsburgh, and Billy used to talk about Linton Garner.

Yeah. Yeah, they all came from Pittsburgh. We had a -- I was playing with Benny Carter at Disneyland, with Billy Eckstine, because I'd done some work for Billy Eckstine, you know, some conducting and album work with him.
Uh-huh.

And Bobby Tucker would go in the booth, you know, and be like the producer. And we'd both begin to learn Billy so well, we knew him, so when he would want to go to Vegas he'd take me with him and leave Bobby back in Jersey, instead of just shipping him out for a day or two.
Uh-huh.
You know. That's expensive.
Sure.

You know. But what I was going to say about the Pittsburgh thing, we were at Disneyland with Benny Carter, and my wife was with me, Ray Brown was playing with us. There was about five or six people there, just talking about Pittsburgh.
Uh-huh.
You know? And somebody said, 'Well, Speedy's from Pittsburgh,' you know. Well, she lived there anyway. She said, 'She was there before you guys even thought about playing music.'
(Laughter)
We had a nice time talking about that then.
Nancy Wilson at the Waldorf Astoria. You conducted for her there. You've conducted for her other times, haven't you?
Yes. Especially on albums.
Yeah. And you've arranged a lot of material for her.
Oh, yes, starting in 1963. And they all sold well, too.
Good.
Yeah, I was living in New York then and they would ship me out here, Capitol Records, you know.
Uh-huh.
Bring me out here to do the writing. I think John Levy was the one that was instrumental in that.
Because John has been Nancy's manager for a long time.
Yeah, but in getting me in the situation with Nancy, because at that time the house writers for Capitol were Billy May and Nelson Riddle, you know.
Uh-huh.

And eventually, when I moved out here, I became the house man, until the managements changed. You know, they changed format, the business format changed, you know. But I had all of the -- and anything that came through there, even Sandler and Young.
Oh.
Yeah, I did two or three albums with them.
Do you have that listed on here? Yeah, you do. Sandler and Young. "Together," "Odds and Ends," "Honey Come Back," "Pretty Things Come in Twos."
Yeah. Let's see, I split one with Billy May and then I did two more by myself, you know?
Uh-huh. And Pat Suzuki.
Oh, boy. Yeah, now -- that's not in chronological order. That's the reason you see me hesitate, to

try to turn my mind off of out here and go way back to New York. Let's see, Pat Suzuki. Well, this was Doc Severinsen again, was in the band. I was the leader. Yes, I know what it was for. It was for the Newport Jazz Festival. We had about seven pieces, you know, and I had to do some writing for it. And we went up to Newport, you know, with Pat.
So you've played Newport with Pat Suzuki and also with Anita O'Day, you were mentioning.
Yes. And with Sarah Vaughan.
With Sarah Vaughan. Anybody else?
I don't know. I think I played there several times with Sarah. Because I was with her so long, you know?
Uh-huh. I see a list here of your recorded compositions. I bet it's not complete. 'Wisteria,' recorded by Johnny Hodges.
Yes.
Wild Bill Davis on, 'Blue Rabbit.'
Yes.
'Rent City,' recorded by Johnny Hodges.
Yeah.
'Shadowy Sands,' recorded by Harry Carney.
Yeah.
Where was that recorded? Was that --
All in New york.
On that HRS label? Or --
Yeah, that was HRS label.
And, 'Minor Mirage,' Ellington small band.
It was Otto Hardwicke.
Uh-huh.
Let me see if I can remember some other stuff. There were a whole lot of HRS things that never got exposed that much, you know. Things -- oh, I can't remember them. Must be at least another ten.

And with record albums, arranging and conducting, for Nancy Wilson on Capitol, we've got, 'Easy,' 'Broadway My Way,' 'Hollywood My Way,' 'The Sounds of Nancy Wilson,' 'Son of a Preacher Man,' and 'Nancy.' And Wes Montgomery, 'Fusion.'
Yes.

Mel Torme, Capitol, 'Raindrops Keep Fallin' On My Head,' and, 'A Time For Us.' Carmen MacRae, on Atlantic, 'The Sound of Silence.' Sarah Vaughan, 'Dreamy,' 'Sarah Vaughan Sings,' and, 'Sarah Vaughan at Mr. Kelly's,' with the Jimmy Jones Trio.
Yeah.
But then you made a lot of 78s with Sarah, didn't you?
Yeah, there were some 78s, but as time went on, -- of course you know we got into the LPs.
Uh-huh.
And it wasn't too long before we got into the LPs, so we didn't do so many 78s, you know.
What label would they have been on?
Music Craft was one. Which, you know, went out of business.
Yeah.
Oh boy, boy, boy. MGM.
Uh-huh. Were you in the ones she did with Billy Eckstine?
Yes. Those were the ones on MGM.

Yeah, MGM, and then there was one LP, a 10 inch LP in a paper jacket on very heavy vinyl material. It wasn't like the -- it must have been one of the earliest LPs. I think it's with Sarah and Billy together, as I remember.
That might be MGM. You know, what they usually do, they re-release them, you know?
Uh-huh.
And we don't know it unless we just happen to browse in a store sometimes and stumble up on them, you know?
Yeah. Then back to albums. Harry Belafonte, 'Jump Up Calypso,' and, 'Midnight Special.'
Yes.
Which was an award winner, you say. What kind of award?

Yes. They called it -- it was done in France. The award -- we got that award from France. Now, it wasn't a jazz thing and it wasn't quite a country and western thing nor was it a calypso album. I don't know what you would call it. It's just a potpourri.
Okay. Then you did Billy Eckstine's Motown album, 'The Love of Ivy.'
Yes.
Is that the one he had the Ellington medley on?
No, he didn't have an Ellington medley on this one.
Ella Fitzgerald and Duke Ellington, on Verve, 'Ella at Duke's Place,' and, 'Ella and Duke at the Cote d'Azur.'
Yes.
With the Jimmy Jones Trio.
Yeah. But 'At Duke's Place,' I did quite a bit of writing.
Uh-huh. Yeah, I remember that. The Jimmy Jones Trio on the Sarah Vaughan album at Mr. Kelly's, who were the members of your trio?
Richard Davis and Roy Haynes.
Uh-huh. And with Ella and Duke at the Cote d'Azur, Jimmy Jones Trio was whom?
Grady Tate and Jim Hugart (PHONETIC).
Okay. And the Joe Williams albums are, "Me and the Blues," "That Kind of Woman," "Jump For Joy," "Joe Williams Sings to You," "Lonely and Sentimental." Is there anything else that isn't on the list?
Well, there's one I played piano on, but all those I just did all the writing and conducting.
Uh-huh.
"A Man Ain't Supposed to Cry."
That's a great album.
Yeah. I was on piano on that.
And then we've got the Sandler and Young albums, and Count Basie, "String Along with Basie."
Yeah. I wrote -- well, they wanted to put Basie with some strings.
Uh-huh.
And I just wrote a couple of scores. Let's see, who else did some work. There were about two or three arrangers jumped on that assignment, you know. And it came off.
And Cannonball Adderley, "Big Man," and, "Love, Sex and the Zodiac."
Yeah, that's right. Cannon and I wrote a tune, "Love, Sex and the Zodiac." That must have been -- oh,
what's the guy's name? Holmes.
Rick Holmes, the disc jockey?
No. Is he disc jockey?
Yeah.
Yeah.
Who was into zodiac things.
Yeah.
Very heavily.
Yeah.
Uh-huh.
And was the other one with Cannonball?
It just lists, "Big Man," and the zodiac album.
Oh, those are the two, yes.
Uh-huh. And Kenny Burrell, "Ellington is Forever."
Yes.
Parts 1 and 2. Volumes 1 and 2.
Yeah.
And, "Duke Ellington, Jazz Party."
Oh, yes.
And, "Ellingtonia, Volume 2, The Impulse Years," Jimmy Jones, pianist.
Wait a minute. Ellington what?
It says, "Ellingtonia, Volume 2, The Impulse Years, J. Jones, pianist, 1973-74, ABC-Impulse Records."
Well, now, I've forgotten some of this stuff.
(Laughter)
Yeah, I did a whole lot of work with the Ellington setup.
Do you remember the Impulse, Ellingtonia album? I'm not familiar with it.
I don't remember it. Oh, there are a lot of things I've done I don't remember.
You don't have the Sinatra album on here, and you're on that one.
Yes, that's right.
Then Milt Jackson, "Feelings." Is that the one with strings?
Yes.
And then there's a note on here that looks like Jerome's handwriting, saying, "A&M Records." What does that mean?
Oh, that --
What have you done at A&M?
Well, when we did the Love You Madly Show, I did some writing there.
Uh-huh.
We recorded it at A&M.
Uh-huh.
And just lately I did some string work over there, because Hugh Masakela and Herb Alpert are having trumpet duets now.
Oh.
You know?
Uh-huh.
So they called me in to drape the strings around their sound, you know.
Uh-huh.
It came out good.
Great. Are there any recent credits that do not appear on your resume, things you've been doing in the last, oh, say, six months or something?
Well, that's one right there.
That's one. What else?
Oh, just did the Tonight Show a lot, you know.
Uh-huh.
And then I'll tell you what I've been doing a lot of too. You write for different acts, like this fellow I'm writing for now, Bob Guillaume, you know?
Uh-huh.
And for Joe Williams. And a lot of times we don't record the stuff. But that's for them to use in Las Vegas and different -- you know, different places. Or they'll.

book Joe with Basie's band, and Joe will call me up for some material a la Basie, you know, so that they can -- you know, they can get the same old chemistry, because that's what the public is looking for. And let's see, I can't -- I can't think of anything too much that is recorded or documented. It's just that I've been doing a lot of that kind of work. In fact the industry has changed around, because a lot of the guys are doing that kind of work now.
Uh-huh.

You know, just for acts. And then another one was Randy Crawford. I can't even think of the -- this was on Warner Brothers. I can't think of what the name of the song was, or whatever the songs were. Oh, I remember. This is a thing at the auditorium -- well, it's further back than what you're asking. I think Quincy Jones, George Benson --
Oh, the World Jazz Association concert at the Shrine Auditorium, in 1975?
Was it that far back?
Uh-huh. November, 1975.
I remember it was in November.
That's right. You conducted --
Yeah.
-- for Randy and what else? Didn't you do something else too on that show?
No, I don't think so. And I conducted once
for Joe Williams, but that was a different show, right at the same place.
Joe was supposed to be on that concert, but he got --
Stranded in London.
Stranded in London, yeah.

When I got there, the -- my schedule was running very tight at the copyist's office, and I began to start pacing the floor, and of course I've got the best in town, the best I've ever had, and they got it done, and when I got to the stage door, there was John Levy outside, pacing the sidewalk. Said, "Joe's in London and Randy's music's not here, our conductor's not here." He started scratching his head, you know?
(Laughter)
But I got there. He wasn't too upset. He had to be a little tense. And he said, "Well, don't you worry about your problems. We've got another big one, because Joe Williams is not going to be here."
Yeah, it was what, snowing in London or something.
I think it was fogged in.
Oh. Something. Yeah, I remember we got the call.
Yeah.
Late. And your copyist that you regard so highly is Bill Hughes, right?
Yeah, that's right. He's -- all that staff over there, they're like co-workers, you know?
Uh-huh.
More than just copyists. They're really orchestrators and everything. And how they get that work out, I do not know. They have all the major shows, you know.
Uh-huh. Yeah, I know, it's amazing, the volume that comes out of there and the high quality, apparently, all the time.
That's right. That's the reason they're in business. The greatest reference, you know?
Uh-huh. You told me a story last night, I think at dinner, about Joe Williams and Count Basie.
(Laughter)
Oh, I don't know whether I should tell it.
I think that's funny. I think you ought to tell that story.

Well, I think they were in -- I heard from Freddie Greene and Thad Jones, so it must be in order. They were in London, I believe. You know, there are some theaters that have false entrances, you know. As you go on stage, you know.
Uh-huh.
One entrance is a false entrance and the other side is the one you're supposed to come on and go off, you know?
Uh-huh.
And Joe saw a lady he liked and he kept talking to her. And Count Basie doesn't talk loud, you know.
I know.

He just walked past Joe and said, 'Joe, don't go in on this side. Go around to the other side.' And Joe didn't seem like he paid him much -- excuse me -- paid him much attention. So Basie started -- he just counted off 'Every Ray,' and that woke Joe up, you know. He stopped talking to the young lady, you know. So when Joe went into this false entrance, there were nothing but stage lights under his feet, and it sounded like gunshots, pow, pow. He's trying to get to the microphone, and the guys in the band, they broke up laughing, because they saw him -- he was stumbling, you know, because the light bulbs were breaking up under his feet. He couldn't hardly walk, you know. And he got there, but this -- I'm trying to describe it as it was described to me. But I can see it, where it would crack somebody up. And Basie was slick. He kept telling Joe to go around the other side, and Joe wasn't paying any attention.
(Laughter)
Always give the leader your full attention, right?
Yeah. But see, Basie, he doesn't go around with a whip. He says it very quietly, you know.
(Laughter)

And Joe was so intent on dating this chick, that's what was wrong with him. He wasn't paying attention. So just like the old saying, to get a mule's attention you've got to hit him in the head with a two by four. So that's what Basie did to Joe. Yeah, that's a funny story.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
